sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H0300.detail: Achischachar is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:10. He is a son of Bilhan, who is himself a son of Jediael. He appears in the genealogy of the Benjamites alongside his brothers Jeusch, Benjamin, Ehud, Kenaana, Zethan, and Tarsis. Nothing is known about his life, deeds, or role; the Bible cites him solely to establish the lineage of the tribe of Benjamin during the period of the divided monarchy (after the schism of the kingdom of Israel).
H0300.origine: His name means "my brother is the dawn" or "brother of the dawn." It is composed of "achi" (my brother) and "shachar" (the dawn, the rising of the day). This type of theophoric name often expressed the hope or spiritual vision of the parents who gave the name, with the dawn being a symbol of renewal and hope in Hebrew thought.
H0300.emploi: Achischachar appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:10, where he is listed among the sons of Bilhan in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. This passage lists the descendants of Jediael, a Benjamite ancestor, without any details about Achischachar's deeds or significance. His mention is part of the larger genealogical record of the tribes of Israel that the chronicler has preserved to maintain the memory of the Israelite lineages.

sens: Officer of King Solomon
Chief of the royal household
H0301.detail: Achischar is a man who served King Solomon during the united reign of Israel and Judah. He held the position of chief of the king's household, meaning he oversaw the administration of the royal palace and the domestic affairs of the court (1 Kings 4:6). This was an important position in the administrative organization of the kingdom.
H0301.origine: The name Achischar literally means "my brother has sung." It is composed of common Hebrew elements: "achi" (my brother) and "shar" (to sing). This name reflects a common practice among the Hebrews of forming proper names from religious or poetic expressions.
H0301.emploi: Achischar is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:6. He is listed among the high officials enumerated by the text to illustrate the sophisticated administrative organization of Solomon's kingdom. This list shows how the king organized his household and public affairs with high-ranking officers responsible for different areas.

sens: Advisor to David during the united monarchy
H0302.detail: Achitophel is a major political figure during the time of King David. He is a man of great wisdom and influence: his counsel to David is said to have authority equal to that of a consultation with God himself (2 Samuel 16:23). He is the father of Eliam and the grandfather of Bathsheba (cf. 2 Samuel 23:34), and he hails from Giloh. During Absalom's rebellion against David, he abandons his master and joins the rebels, convinced that the young prince's counsel will prevail. However, Absalom prefers to listen to Hushai and rejects Achitophel's strategies: seeing his advice dismissed and understanding that it will lead to defeat, he takes his own life (2 Samuel 17:23).
H0302.origine: His name means in Hebrew "my brother is folly" or "my brother is foolish." It is a symbolic name that, in hindsight, aptly describes his fate: his defection from David and his suicide present him as a man guided by faulty judgment, despite his apparent wisdom.
H0302.emploi: Achitophel appears 17 times in the Bible, solely in the accounts of Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 15–17) and in David's administrative lists (1 Chronicles 27:33–34). At the beginning of the rebellion, he is the architect of the plot and advises Absalom confidently; his initial opinions are shrewd and terrifying for David (2 Samuel 17:1–4). But this is a decisive turning point: when Absalom instead listens to Hushai, who recommends patience, Achitophel realizes that all is lost. The text reveals that the Lord intended to nullify Achitophel's good counsel to bring disaster upon Absalom, showing that human wisdom, no matter how great, cannot prevail against the will of God.
H0302.portee: The story of Achitophel teaches the reader that betrayal and pride, even in a brilliant man, lead to destruction. It also shows that God governs history: He can render the most wise counsel ineffective if it serves His purposes. Finally, it invites consideration that true wisdom lies not in intelligence or personal prestige, but in obedience to God.

sens: Canaanite city allotted to the tribe of Asher
H0303.detail: Achlal is a Canaanite city that God assigned to the tribe of Asher during the division of the promised land. The name literally means "fertile place," which corresponds to its location in Canaan. In Judges 1:31, it is mentioned among the cities whose inhabitants were not driven out by Asher, despite the divine order to completely conquer their territory.
H0303.origine: The Hebrew name אַחְלָב (Achlal) means "fertile place" or "fruitful spot." It is also known by the variant חֶבֶל (Mahalab). The precise location of this city in Canaan is not definitively identified from current archaeological sources, but it was situated in the coastal region of northern Canaan.
H0303.emploi: Achlal appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 1:31. It is listed there among Canaanite cities that the tribe of Asher was supposed to conquer but did not eliminate. This passage is part of the account of the incomplete conquests of the Israelite tribes after their entry into Canaan, showing how Asher, like other tribes, did not fully obey the command for total possession of the territory.

sens: Son of Sheshan in the genealogy of Judah
H0304G.detail: Achlaï is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. He appears in the genealogical list in the book of Chronicles as the son of Sheshan (1 Chronicles 2:31). He is the father of Attai, who became one of the mighty and renowned warriors of King David.
H0304G.origine: The name Achlaï literally means "Oh! if only!" in ancient Hebrew. It expresses an interjection or a wish, making it a rare and memorable name for an ancestor. It is an example of a theophoric or expressive name, common in the genealogies of Israel.
H0304G.emploi: Achlaï appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:31, where he is listed in the genealogy of Judah established after the exile. Although he is little known, his significance lies in the fact that his son Attai distinguished himself as one of the mighty men (elite warriors) of King David, demonstrating the influence of this lineage over generations.

sens: Father of Zabad, one of David's warriors
H0304H.detail: Achlaï is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:41, where he is identified as the father of Zabad. Zabad appears in the list of "mighty men" of David, those warriors who served the king of Israel during the period of the divided monarchy. Nothing else is known about him other than this paternity.
H0304H.origine: The name Achlaï literally means "Oh! may it please God!" or "if only I had...!" in Hebrew, expressing a wish or regret. It is a particular name that likely reflects the emotion of the parent at the time of the child's birth.
H0304H.emploi: Achlaï appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:41. This passage lists the "mighty men" or "warriors" who fought alongside King David. Zabad, the son of Achlaï, is named among these heroes who marked the military history of Israel. This single mention places him in the time of the divided monarchy, during David's reign.

sens: Intense wish, strong desire
Regret or lament for the absence of something
Call to God for transformation
Expression of a deep aspiration
H0305.detail:
1. The word expresses an intense, passionate wish: the little Israelite servant ardently wishes that her master, General Naaman, could meet the prophet Elisha and be healed of his leprosy (2 Kings 5:3). It is stronger than a simple wish; it is the exclamation of a heart that strongly desires something.
2. It can also mark a deep aspiration, a prayer for God to transform or guide a situation. In Psalm 119:5, the psalmist cries out: "Oh that my actions may be directed to keep your statutes!" — it is a heartfelt call to God for his life to change and for each of his actions to honor the divine Law.
3. This interjection gives voice to the most vivid feelings of the heart: a desire that seems almost impossible, but for which one begs God to realize, or a regret for what is lacking and that one would ardently wish for.
H0305.origine: The interjection אַחֲלַי (achalay) is formed from a root expressing desire, wish. It is the raw expression of an intense feeling: not a polite request, but an exclamation that rises from the heart. It appears in moments of strong emotion, where the speaker expresses a nearly desperate wish.
H0305.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. First in 2 Kings 5:3, from the mouth of a compassionate little Syrian servant: she wishes that her master Naaman be healed by the prophet of Israel. Then in Psalm 119:5, where the psalmist addresses God: he longs for his entire life to be directed according to the divine Law. In both cases, the interjection marks not a quiet request, but a burning desire, an aspiration that engages the whole being.
H0305.portee: This word reminds us that prayer is not primarily a politeness, but the true expression of our deepest desires. It invites us to cry out to God with sincerity and passion, without fear of showing our most intimate aspirations — to heal the affliction, to live according to His will — as the servant and the psalmist do. It is a language from heart to heart.

sens: Precious stone of purple or violet color
Stone of the high priest's breastplate, third row
H0306.detail:
1. The amethyst is a precious stone, probably purple or violet in color, although its exact identification is debated (it could also be a reddish or brownish jasper). It is a hard, shiny, and valuable stone, used as jewelry.
2. In the breastplate of judgment worn by the high priest, the amethyst held a special place: it was in the third row, alongside an opal and an agate (Exodus 28:19 and 39:12). This breastplate contained twelve stones representing the twelve tribes of Israel, and thus the amethyst was one of the twelve sacred stones of the high priest.
H0306.origine: The Hebrew word אַחְלָמָה (ahlama) probably comes from a root meaning "dream" or "vision," or perhaps from an older root denoting color or brightness. The term has been transmitted through ancient languages and borrowed from Greek in the Septuagint, where it becomes ἀμέθυστος (améthystos). The French word "améthyste" descends directly from this ancient Greek word.
H0306.emploi: The Hebrew word אַחְלָמָה appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the book of Exodus, during the description of the high priest's breastplate. These two occurrences (Exodus 28:19 and 39:12) are parallel: one describes the design of the breastplate given by God to Moses, the other its actual realization by Bezalel. In both cases, the amethyst occupies exactly the same place — the third row of the breastplate, with the opal and the agate. The usage is therefore very restricted and liturgical: this stone appears only in this specific priestly context.
H0306.portee: The amethyst reminds us that the worship and priesthood of the people of Israel were richly adorned and precious in the eyes of God. The twelve stones of the high priest's breastplate bore the names of the twelve tribes engraved upon them, symbolizing that the high priest carried all the people before the Lord. This splendor of sacred ornaments reflects the importance and dignity of the priestly mediation, and foreshadows the glory of Christ's ministry as our Great High Priest.

sens: Capital of Media, historical city of the Persian empire
H0307.detail: Achmetha is the capital of the province of Media in the Persian empire. It was conquered by Cyrus around 550 B.C. and later became a summer residence for Persian kings. In the book of Ezra, it is at Achmetha that the decree of Cyrus authorizing the reconstruction of the Jerusalem temple is discovered (Ezra 6:2).
H0307.origine: The Akkadian and Persian name Achmetha designates this great city, also known by the Greek name "Ecbatana." It was a major administrative center of the empire of the Medes and then the Persians.
H0307.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 6:2, in the context of the return of the Jews from exile. It is in the archives of Achmetha that the Persian authorities find the decree of Cyrus authorizing the reconstruction of the temple. This passage shows the historical importance of this city as a seat of Persian power and a place for the preservation of royal decrees.
H0307.portee: This account reminds us that God controls the hearts of foreign kings and uses imperial administration to accomplish His plan for the restoration of His people and His temple. The discovery of the decree at Achmetha demonstrates how God continues His work even in the heart of pagan empires.

sens: Father of Eliphelet, one of David's warriors
H0308.detail: Achasbai is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:34, as the father of Eliphelet, who is among the thirty-seven elite warriors of David. His name literally means "brother of those who surround me," a poetic expression suggesting a shared or communal life.
H0308.origine: The Hebrew name Achasbai is composed of elements that evoke the idea of belonging to a group or community. It is a personal name borne by a man from the period of the united monarchy in Israel, under the reign of King David.
H0308.emploi: Achasbai appears only once in the biblical texts, in 2 Samuel 23:34. He is cited in the official list of David's heroes, a historical document that enumerates the king's most valiant soldiers. His only known biblical role is to be the father of Eliphelet, a respected warrior of David.

sens: Let time pass before acting or arriving
Stay behind, linger somewhere for a long time
Delay someone, slow them down in their action
Defer, not rush to do something
Wait slowly, be patient without haste
H0309.detail:
1. To delay means to let time pass before doing something or before arriving at a destination. Sisera's mother watches from the window asking, "Why does his chariot delay in coming?" (Judges 5:28) — she worries that the return is taking a long time.
2. To stay behind means to linger or remain somewhere, not to progress. This is also the meaning of the word in Psalms 127:2 where one "lies down late" — extending the hour of rest beyond the normal.
3. To delay someone means to slow them down or prevent them from advancing. Abraham's servant says to Rebecca's family: "Do not delay me, since the Lord has made my journey successful" (Genesis 24:56) — he wants them not to hinder him in his mission.
4. To defer or postpone: God "does not defer toward one who hates Him" (Deuteronomy 7:10) — He does not postpone His punishment, He does not hesitate.
5. To wait slowly expresses a certain patience mixed with passivity — one stays behind, does not rush.
H0309.origine: The Hebrew verb אָחַר (achar) comes from a root that evokes the idea of staying behind, of dragging. The family of the word also includes אַחֲרִית (acharit, the end), what comes after, and אַחַר (achar, after, behind). The basic image is of something or someone who stays behind, who does not keep pace with others. This word can also literally mean to remain sitting or lying down for a long time.
H0309.emploi: The verb appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible. Genesis and Deuteronomy use it mainly in the sense of "not delaying" or "not deferring" in urgent situations (the servant who does not want to be delayed, God who does not defer His justice). The Psalms use it to express anxiety over a delay ("My God, do not delay!" in 40:18) or to describe a habit that stretches (lying down late). Isaiah places it in divine promises: "Salvation will not delay" (46:13). Habakkuk uses the same verb to say that the vision "will not delay" (2:3). The context varies: urgency, impatience, waiting, delay, or simple prolongation of an action.
H0309.portee: This word teaches us the importance of not deferring when God calls. It is also a comforting word: God does not delay in helping His servants, even when it seems long in our eyes. It invites the believer to vigilance: not to linger in laziness or disobedience, but to move forward with God without dragging.

sens: Behind, at the back (place)
Then, later (time)
Follow, pursue someone or something
As a result of, due to
Behind, beyond (in a spatial or temporal sense)
H0310A.detail:
1. Behind, at the back (place): the word designates what is located at the back, behind. Thus, in Exodus 15:20, Miriam walks in front and the women come "after her," meaning behind her as they follow.
2. Then, later (time): it indicates a succession in time, what comes after an event. In Genesis 5:4, "after the birth of Seth," Adam lived another eight hundred years: the word marks chronological order.
3. Follow, pursue someone or something: it expresses the action of going after someone, catching up with them. In 2 Kings 14:19, one "pursues" the king to Lachish: it is a hunt, an armed pursuit.
4. As a result of, due to: it introduces a consequence or reason. In Proverbs 20:25, reflecting "after" making a vow means reflecting as a consequence, too late.
5. Behind, beyond (in a spatial or temporal sense): it can evoke what exceeds, what is yet to come, or what extends beyond.
H0310A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses movement backward and the idea of succession. Its fundamental image is that of a line of march: something or someone that comes after, that follows. The temporal sense ("then") naturally derives from the spatial sense ("behind"), as in biblical thought, time is represented as a succession where what comes after follows what precedes, like in a procession.
H0310A.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, with 664 occurrences. It appears as early as Genesis and in all historical and wisdom books. Its temporal use is massive: "after" an event occurs, the genealogies of Genesis 5 constantly use it to mark generations ("after the birth of Seth"). Its use of movement and pursuit appears in war or flight narratives (Joshua 10:19: "pursue your enemies"). In 2 Samuel 2:22, in a dialogue, "then" takes the meaning of "after that" in the consequence or temporality of an act. The word can also be a preposition, adverb, or conjunction, making it a fundamental grammatical tool for chaining events and constructing the narrative.
H0310A.portee: This word helps us understand how the Bible tells the story: by following the succession of generations, events, actions, and their consequences. It reminds us that time flows, that things happen in order, and that we are called to perceive in this unfolding the hand of God. It is also a word of movement: to follow or pursue someone means to engage after them; it evokes our call to follow the Lord, to walk in His footsteps.

sens: after, in a time that follows
as a result of, behind
H0310B.detail: 1. "Then" designates what comes after in time: after an action or a word, what occurs in return or as a consequence. In Proverbs 28:23, he who rebukes others frankly will find "then" more favor — meaning that as a result of this honesty, favor will come. 2. The word also evokes the idea of a rear guard, of what follows someone or something in space, hence the image of "after" and "behind": it is the mark of time that flows.
H0310B.origine: This Hebrew adverb comes from the root אחר "after, behind." It fundamentally expresses order: what comes after in time or space. The adverb אַחֲרַי retains this primary sense of after, of succession.
H0310B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Old Testament (Proverbs 28:23). It is used there to express a temporal or logical consequence: after someone has acted honestly in rebuking others, it will result in increased favor. It is a promise of future blessing linked to honest and courageous conduct.
H0310B.portee: This passage teaches that honesty and sincere correction, even if they seem difficult at the moment, produce lasting favor "then." For the believer, it is an invitation to prefer truth over flattery, trusting that God rewards this integrity in due time.

sens: then, in the time that follows
in succession, following someone or something
H0311.detail:
1. This word indicates a succession in time: it designates what comes after a given moment or period. In Daniel 2:29, the king asks to know "what will be after this time," meaning what will happen in the future. It is the time that follows the present or another event.
2. The word also marks a succession in an order or series. In Daniel 7:24, a king "will arise after them," coming after the ten kings who preceded him. This emphasizes the order of appearance: after the first, comes a new king with his own characteristics.
H0311.origine: אַחַר (achar) comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally expresses the idea of what comes behind or after. The word evokes the image of a line where what follows comes after what precedes. In Aramaic, the form אַחַר (achar) directly retains this Hebrew meaning. It is a very common adverb of time and position in both Semitic languages.
H0311.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Aramaic New Testament of Daniel, always in a temporal sense. In Daniel 2:29 and 2:45, it concerns the succession of future events that God reveals to Nebuchadnezzar: what will happen "after" the current moment. In Daniel 7:24, it describes the order of appearance of kings in the eschatological vision: a new king comes "after" the first ten. In all cases, it marks a break in time or the order of events.
H0311.portee: This small word reminds us that history follows God's plan: after one event comes another, according to a succession that God knows in advance and reveals to his prophets. For the reader, this reinforces the idea that nothing escapes divine sovereignty, not even the future order of things. The word invites us to trust God's word about what is to come.

sens: What is distinct, different, separate from the first thing
What comes after, following in an order, a succession
The additional person or thing, in addition to the one already mentioned
One who is not from our group, our people, our god
H0312.detail:
1. The word designates what is different or distinct from a first thing. In Genesis 4:25, Eve gives birth to "another son" in place of Abel: this son is distinct from the first and replaces him. It is a simple distinction between two beings or two objects.

2. "Other" also indicates what follows in a succession, a temporal or spatial succession. In Genesis 8:10, Noah sends out the dove, then sends it "again" (or "another time"): the action repeats in order. In Leviticus 14:42, stones from a house are removed and replaced by "others."

3. The word can express the idea of a supplement, of "more": there is a first thing, then another in addition. In Genesis 29:27, Jacob asks for another seven years to serve for Rachel, "another term."

4. In religious texts, "other" applies to gods different from the true God: "other gods" in Exodus 20:3 and Joshua 23:16 refer to foreign deities that the peoples worship and that the Israelites must never serve.
H0312.origine: The root הברא (Hebrew, which literally means "behind") is the origin of the word; "other" first evokes what comes after, what follows. The word can also express what is beyond, what is distinct or separate. In biblical vocabulary, "other" naturally opposes "one" or "the first," and also serves to designate the foreigner, the outsider.
H0312.emploi: The word "other" appears 161 times in the Old Testament, mainly to distinguish beings or things: sons (Genesis 4:25), inheritances (Numbers 36:9), or peoples. It frequently returns in the expression "other gods" to designate foreign deities; the biblical text repeats this notably in Exodus, Deuteronomy, and Joshua to remind of the prohibition of idolatry. "Other" is also used in concrete contexts of succession (a second house, a second wife, a second field), marking repetition or addition. Sometimes, the word simply designates what is distinct or foreign (the neighbor, the outsider).
H0312.portee: This word reminds believers of two major truths: first, that everything that is not of God, everything that replaces Him, is "other"—that is, idolatry. By constantly reminding that serving "other gods" is forbidden, the Bible confronts the reader with a radical choice. Secondly, "other" speaks to us of the uniqueness of God: there is only one true God, no "other" before whom to bow. For the believer, this word invites rejection of anything that diverts from God alone.

sens: man of the tribe of Benjamin
H0313.detail: Acher is a character from the Old Testament belonging to the tribe of Benjamin. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:12, where he is identified as the father of Huschim. His name appears in the genealogy of the sons of Beniamin, who himself was a son of Benjamin.
H0313.origine: The name Acher literally means "one who follows" or "following," deriving from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of following someone or coming after. This type of genealogical name was common in the tribal lineages of Israel to mark descendants and familial ties.
H0313.emploi: Acher appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 7:12. He is presented as one of the descendants of Benjamin, recorded in the genealogical register of the tribe. Although little documented in the Bible, his inclusion in these genealogical lists shows that his lineage was recognized and counted among the Benjaminite families, particularly at the time of the divided monarchy.

sens: Who comes last in a succession, in time or in order
Who is at the back, towards the west or in the background
Who belongs to a later, future, or coming time
H0314.detail:
1. The most common meaning: what closes a series, what comes last. When Jacob places his maidservants, then Leah, he places "finally" Rachel, that is, last (Genesis 33:2). Or again: the "last" orders of David are those he gave shortly before his death (1 Chronicles 23:27). The word also designates one who arrives after others, at the end of the line.
2. A spatial meaning: what is behind, particularly towards the west or in the background. The "western sea" is the Mediterranean, which extends to the west of Israel (Deuteronomy 34:2). This usage comes from the image of one who is "behind" you.
3. A temporal meaning looking towards the future: what is later or to come. The "future generations" are those who will be born after us (Psalms 78:6). It is also the meaning when God says: "I am the last," meaning the one who comes last, who dominates all that follows (Isaiah 44:6).
H0314.origine: The Hebrew word אַחֲרוֹן comes from the root אחר (achar), which means "to be behind." The starting image is that of what stands in the back, at the end. The same root generates the word אַחַר (achar), "after" or "behind," and אָחוֹר (achor), "back." This is why the word can mean both "last in time" and "back in space": it is always a question of relative position.
H0314.emploi: The word appears 48 times in the Old Testament, especially in historical and poetic books. The temporal meaning is the most frequent: to designate the last act, the last day, the last generation. We see it in the fixed formulas of Chronicles, which summarize the history of a king by "his first and last actions" (2 Chronicles 28:26). The spatial meaning (back, west) is less common but clear: the Mediterranean is "the western sea" (Deuteronomy 34:2). Isaiah uses the word theologically: God is "the first and the last," affirming His dominion over all time and history (Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12). The word can also qualify a person: the last wife of a man, or the youngest son.
H0314.portee: This word helps the reader grasp how God dominates time. When God says "I am the last," He is not speaking of weakness or delay, but of His omnipotence: He is the one who comes after all, who will judge, who will accomplish everything. Meditating on this word invites the believer to see history as going somewhere, towards an accomplishment, and to recognize that God masters this "last" day. It is a word of hope and assurance.

sens: Son of Benjamin, mentioned in the genealogies of Israel
H0315.detail: Achrach is one of the sons of Benjamin listed in the genealogy of the twelve tribes. He appears in 1 Chronicles 8:1, where he is designated as the third son of Benjamin, after Bela and Ashbel. This character is mentioned only once in the Bible and has no particular story: his name simply appears in the list of ancestors of the tribe of Benjamin.
H0315.origine: The name Achrach (אַחְרַח in Hebrew) literally means "a brother who follows" or "a brother from behind," composed of אַח ("brother") and רַח ("who follows"). It is a typical patronymic name in ancient Israelite genealogies, where names often reflect a circumstance of birth or a position in the sibling order.
H0315.emploi: Achrach is mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 8:1, as part of the genealogical census of the tribe of Benjamin at the time of the return from exile. The biblical text clearly establishes his lineage — son of Benjamin — and his rank among the children of Benjamin. No event or specific action is reported about him; his name has been preserved in the genealogical records of Israel to attest to the continuity of Benjamin's descent.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah
Son of Harum
H0316.detail: Acharchel is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is presented as the son of Harum and is part of the genealogy of the descendants of Caleb (1 Chronicles 4:8).
H0316.origine: The name means "an army that follows" or "a multitude that follows," composed of Hebrew elements evoking the idea of pursuing or following. This type of theophoric or symbolic names was common in Israel to express hopes or blessings.
H0316.emploi: Acharchel appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:8. He is listed in the genealogical record of the tribe of Judah, in the branch descended from Caleb. His father is Harum, and he is mentioned among the families of that time in the divided kingdom.

sens: distinct, different from the first
that comes after, that follows
additional, in addition to others
H0317.detail:
1. The word denotes something distinct or different from a first thing. In Daniel 2:39, Nebuchadnezzar receives the interpretation that "after you, there will arise another kingdom, lesser than yours": this second kingdom will be different from the first, with its own characteristics.
2. It can also mark the order of succession or what comes after. In Daniel 7:6, the prophet sees another beast after the first, and then in Daniel 7:8, a "little horn" that arises among the ten horns: these terms emphasize that it is a new reality that comes after the previous one.
3. The word can express the idea of an addition or multiplicity: Daniel 7:20 speaks of this "other horn that had come up" distinguishing it from the three that had disappeared, showing that it is additional to the first ones.
H0317.origine: This Aramaic word is the direct equivalent of the Hebrew *achèr* (אַחֵר, H0312). It derives from a primitive Semitic root expressing the idea of difference or otherness. In the biblical world, "other" always opposes "the same" or "the first," and it gives rise to the idea of a sequence or progression.
H0317.emploi: This word appears only in the book of Daniel, concentrated in chapters 2 and 7 where Daniel interprets the visions of the king and receives his own vision of the four beasts. It is used five times to mark the reigns or powers that succeed one another in history: first the four kingdoms of Nebuchadnezzar's vision, then the four beasts of Daniel's vision. Each time, "other" introduces a new stage or new power, highlighting the succession of empires and the progression of time until the day of judgment.
H0317.portee: This word helps the reader grasp that the history of nations is not chaotic but ordered: each empire comes *after* the previous one according to a divine plan. For the Christian, these visions remind that God controls the unfolding of worldly powers and judges them. The repetition of "other" also emphasizes that the passing world will be replaced by a new order, that of the Son of Man.

sens: that comes last, after the others
that occurs at the end of a succession or enumeration
H0318.detail:
1. The word denotes what comes last in an order or succession. When King Nebuchadnezzar lists the wise men before whom he presents his dream, Daniel comes "last" (Daniel 4:8): he is presented after all the other advisors, as the final one in an enumeration.
2. It can also evoke the end of a period of time or the ultimate event in a series. The image is that of what closes a march, which finishes a procession or a list.
H0318.origine: This Hebrew adverb comes from a root meaning "after" or "behind." It is built on a word that denotes the extremity, the end, or what remains (the "remnant"). That is why it naturally expresses the idea of what comes at the end, as if looking back at a procession to designate the one who closes the march.
H0318.emploi: This word is very rare in the Hebrew Bible: it appears only once, in Daniel 4:8. In this royal and narrative context, it serves to structure the enumeration of the wise men of the Babylonian king, marking that Daniel is presented after all the others. Its use emphasizes the hierarchical or ceremonial order of the presentation, while implying that the one who arrives "last" may be the most important (as is often the case in biblical narratives).
H0318.portee: This word reminds us that apparent order is not always the order of importance. Daniel, presented "last," turns out to be the one who possesses true wisdom and the ability to interpret the king's dream. This invites the reader not to judge by appearance or position, but to recognize that God often places His most important servants outside the honors of the world.

sens: The outcome or final result of something
The moment when something ends or concludes
The future, what will happen in the time to come
What remains afterward, the continuation or descendants
The destiny or fate of a person
H0319.detail:
1. The outcome or final result of something: it is the culmination, what ultimately happens. In Proverbs 14:12, it is said of a bad path that "its end is the way of death" — meaning where it leads in the end. It can also refer to an event that occurs: in Deuteronomy 32:29, the text asks people to reflect on "what will happen to them".
2. The moment when something ends or concludes: it is the end of a duration, of a situation. In Proverbs 25:8, "at the end you will not know what to do" means when the matter is finished and it will be too late. It is the temporal extremity of a thing.
3. The future, what will happen in the time to come: particularly the distant or prophetic future. In Genesis 49:1, Jacob announces "what will happen to you in the latter days" — he speaks of what will come afterward. In Isaiah 46:10, God says "from the beginning the end", speaking of the entire course of history.
4. What remains afterward, the continuation or descendants: this refers to future generations or posterity. In Psalms 109:13, it is said that the posterity of the wicked should be "cut off", meaning their line does not continue.
5. The destiny or fate of a person: what will ultimately happen to them. In Lamentations 1:9, it is said that Jerusalem "did not consider her end", meaning her unfortunate future or the disaster that awaited her.
H0319.origine: The word comes from the root "achre" which means "back, behind". The "achrith" is therefore literally what comes "behind", either in the order of time (what comes after) or in the order of space (what is at the end, at the extremity). This root also appears in words describing the back or posterior side. The word appears in Aramaic with the same meaning.
H0319.emploi: The word appears about 60 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books and among the prophets. In Proverbs, it often denotes the concrete outcome of an action or a path — good or bad. In the prophetic books, notably in Jeremiah, Isaiah, and Daniel, it takes on an eschatological hue: it speaks of the "last days", of what will happen at the end of history. In Job 42:12, Job prospers "at his end" more than at the beginning, speaking of his final fate. The word can also simply denote the conclusion of a narrative (Ecclesiastes 7:8: "the end of a thing is better than its beginning").
H0319.portee: This word reminds us that every path, every human action has an end, an outcome — that we must consider it before acting. It also speaks to us of the future and God's plan: for the believer, it invites trust in the one who knows the future and guides everything according to His counsel. The end of the wicked and the end of the righteous are not the same — this encourages the heart in the face of present injustices.

sens: the period that comes after, the future
the course of future events
what will unfold in the remaining time
H0320.detail:
1. The word designates what comes after, the future: what is placed after the present in the order of time. In Daniel 2:28, King Nebuchadnezzar receives a revelation about "the latter days" — what will happen after the present moment when he reigns.

2. More broadly, it evokes the course of future events, the unfolding of history to come. It is the idea that the future is not fixed but will unfold progressively according to a plan that God knows and can reveal.
H0320.origine: The word comes from the root "achar" (אַחַר) which means "after, behind". The suffix "-it" makes it an abstract feminine noun: literally "what is after". In Aramaic (the language of Daniel 2:28), it is the corresponding form of the Hebrew word acharit (אַחֲרִית), which also appears in other biblical books to refer to the last or final times. The root expresses the idea of succession in time.
H0320.emploi: This Aramaic word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 2:28. Daniel uses it to explain to the king that God reveals "what will happen in the latter days". In this context, it is not only about a distant or eschatological future, but about the ordinary course of future events that God can unveil through prophecy. The context of the dream of the four metals shows that this "latter" includes several reigns and dynasties that will succeed one another.
H0320.portee: This passage reminds the Christian that God knows and controls the future — not by fatalism, but because He is the Lord of it. Even the history of nations and the powers of the world unfolds under His gaze. For the believer, this invites trust in divine providence rather than fearing the uncertain.

sens: Distinct, different, not the same
A person or thing in place of another
What is additional, supplementary
H0321.detail:
1. "Other" designates what is distinct or different from the first thing: it is not the same, it is a separate reality. In Daniel 7:24, when another king arises after the first ten, he is explicitly "different from the first ones".
2. The word also expresses replacement or substitution: a person or thing that takes the place of another. In Daniel 5:17, Daniel invites the king to offer his gifts to another in place of himself.
3. In a broader sense, "other" can mean what is added, what is supplementary. The context of the kingdoms in Daniel 2:44 and 7:24 shows additional beings or powers that come after the first ones.
H0321.origine: The Aramaic word אׇחֳרָן (ochoran) comes from the same root as the Hebrew אַחֵר (acher, "other"), which expresses the fundamental idea of distinction or separation. The underlying Hebrew root literally evokes what comes "after" or "beside", hence the sense of otherness. This same family of words appears in various forms in biblical Hebrew, always to express the notion of difference or succession.
H0321.emploi: The Aramaic word ochoran appears only in the book of Daniel (5 occurrences). It is regularly used to mark an opposition or distinction: between a god and another god unable to deliver (Daniel 3:29), between a king and another who arises after him (Daniel 7:24), between a people and another people that would dominate the kingdom (Daniel 2:44). Only once (Daniel 2:11), the word is translated as "difficult": the basic meaning ("other", "distinct") shifts toward the idea that the requested thing is of a different, extraordinary nature, beyond common reach. This is a rhetorical use of the same principle: what is not like ordinary things.
H0321.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize the absolute distinction between the living God and all other gods (Daniel 3:29), between the kingdom of God which will never be destroyed and all human empires (Daniel 2:44). It emphasizes the clear separation between divine and human orders, fundamental to faith in one unique and supreme God.

sens: To move backward, facing away from the direction of movement
To fall or topple backward
To return to a previous state, to bring back
H0322.detail:
1. To advance backward, turning one's back to the direction one is going. This is to walk backward, as Shem and Japheth covered their father: they "walked backward" to avoid seeing his nakedness (Genesis 9:23).
2. To fall or topple violently backward. He collapses "backward" from his seat and breaks his neck (1 Samuel 4:18).
3. To bring something or someone back, or to return to a previous state. The shadow of the sun "goes back" ten degrees (2 Kings 20:10), returning to its former position. God can also "bring back" the heart of a people (1 Kings 18:37), turning them back to Him.
H0322.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "behind, backward." It primarily expresses the spatial idea: what is at the back, behind oneself. From this arises the verb: to go backward, to retreat. The basic image is that of bodily movement: to turn or move in the opposite direction to one's usual path.
H0322.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly to describe physical movements. In Genesis 9:23, it refers to walking backward. In 1 Samuel 4:18, it evokes a backward fall. For the degrees of Ahaz (2 Kings 20:10-11 and Isaiah 38:8), it speaks of the return of the shadow of the sun, a miraculous event. The word can also mean "to bring back," "to return" someone to something, as when God brings back the heart of the people (1 Kings 18:37). The meaning thus oscillates between spatial movement (going backward) and figurative movement (bringing back, returning).
H0322.portee: This word invites the reader to see how God masters time and space: He can make the shadow of the sun retreat, bring back hearts. It also teaches us humility and respect: Shem and Japheth walk backward, eyes averted, out of modesty toward their father. It reminds us that going backward is not always a weakness, but sometimes an act of obedience or wisdom.

sens: Governor of a large province of the Persian Empire
High royal official invested with administrative and military authority
H0323.detail:
1. A satrap is a province of the Persian Empire, and the governor who administers it on behalf of the king. It is a high office: the satrap covers a vast territory populated by diverse peoples (Esther 8:9 mentions one hundred twenty-seven provinces "from India to Ethiopia"). The satrap must enforce royal orders, apply the king's decrees, and collect taxes. When King Ahasuerus orders the massacre of the Jews by Haman, it is to the satraps that the secretaries address the decree: it is up to them to implement it in their respective provinces (Esther 3:12).
2. By extension, the term designates any high official tasked with governing on behalf of the king. The satraps appear alongside governors and chiefs, forming a hierarchy of Persian administration (Esther 9:3). They possess sufficient prestige and power that the Jews, threatened with destruction, had reason to count on their respect for Mordecai (Esther 9:3).
H0323.origine: The Hebrew word אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפַּן (achashdarvan) is borrowed from Old Persian *khshathrapavan*, composed of *khshathra* ("power, domain") and *pavan* ("protector"). It is a technical term of Persian administration, transliterated as such in the Hebrew texts of the books of Ezra and Esther, which recount the history of the Jews under Persian rule. The word also appears in Aramaic (achashdarfnin, H0324).
H0323.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Bible, all in the books of Ezra and Esther, which deal with the Persian political context. In Ezra 8:36, the satraps honor Ezra and his mission by bringing offerings to the temple in Jerusalem. In Esther 3:12 and 8:9, they are the recipients of royal decrees: Haman and then Mordecai send their orders through the satraps to be conveyed to all the peoples of their provinces. In Esther 9:3, the satraps "support" the Jews, demonstrating that Mordecai's influence at the king's court extends to the highest levels of administration.
H0323.portee: This word helps the reader understand the structure of Persian power and the political stakes of the book of Esther: the Jews are not abandoned in the face of Haman's malice, for God places Mordecai in a position of influence, capable of reaching the satraps themselves. It is also a reminder that God governs the history of nations through paths that we do not always see immediately.

sens: Governor of a province of the Persian Empire
High-ranking official tasked with administering a territory on behalf of the king
A figure invested with recognized and respected authority
H0324.detail:
1. In the Persian Empire, a satrap is a province, and a satrap is the man whom the king entrusts with the governance of that region. It is a very high official title: Darius established one hundred twenty satraps throughout his kingdom (Daniel 6:1), and among them, three chiefs hold a controlling position (Daniel 6:2).

2. The satrap is an administrator: he is accountable, manages order and justice in his territory, and participates in official court events. At the dedication of the statue of Nebuchadnezzar, the satraps gather alongside the administrators, governors, and judges (Daniel 3:2-3).

3. It is also a title of prestige and power. Daniel surpasses in wisdom the chiefs and the other satraps (Daniel 6:3), to the point that the king considers establishing him over the entire kingdom. The satraps represent the administrative elite of the empire.
H0324.origine: The Aramaic word אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנִין comes from Old Persian *xšaçapāvan*, where *xšaçā* means "kingdom" or "province" and *pāvan* means "protector" or "guardian." It literally means "protector of the kingdom" or "guardian of the province." This technical term designates a historically well-documented institution of Persian administration: the division of the empire into provinces governed by satraps accountable to the king.
H0324.emploi: The word appears only in the book of Daniel (9 occurrences), exclusively during the Persian domination over Babylon, with Nebuchadnezzar and then Darius. It is always used to designate high-ranking state officials: either during official ceremonies where they are summoned en masse (Daniel 3:2-3, 3:27), or in the administrative context where Darius creates a network to govern (Daniel 6:1-7). The word never changes meaning: it is always a title of very high rank, distinct from the simple governors or administrators mentioned in the same verses.
H0324.portee: The figure of the satrap reminds the reader that God reigns over all empires and their authorities. Daniel, though a foreigner and an exile, surpasses in integrity the satraps of the Persian kingdom: this teaches that wisdom and righteousness come from God, and that no human authority, even the highest, can prevail against faithfulness to God. It is an encouragement for the believer placed in a context where he must serve powers that do not acknowledge the Lord.

sens: king of Persia during the Exile and Return
one who reigns over a vast empire in western Asia
figure of human authority in the face of God's plans
H0325.detail:
1. Ahasuerus is a Persian king who reigns during the Exile and Return of Israel. His name first appears in the book of Ezra at the time when the adversaries of the Jews write against them (Ezra 4:6). Historians identify him as Xerxes, a real king of Persia whose reign spans several decades.
2. He is a sovereign of great power, master of an empire extending from India to Ethiopia (Esther 1:1-2). The book of Esther shows him giving orders to his servants, repudiating his queen Vashti who refuses to obey him (Esther 1:15), and summoning all the young women of the kingdom to choose a new wife — presenting him as an absolute monarch whose word is law.
3. Ahasuerus also embodies the powerful man who is easily manipulated, unaware of the true stakes surrounding him. Haman persuades him to issue a death decree against all the Jews in his empire (Esther 3:7), without the king understanding the true purpose of his favorite. It is only through Queen Esther that he discovers the plot and reverses the decree (Esther 8:1)—showing how God governs history beyond the wills of kings.
H0325.origine: The name Ahasuerus comes from the Hebrew אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ (a-chash-vé-rosh), which tradition interprets as meaning "one who will be silent and poor" or a close variant. It is a transcription of the real Persian name Khshayarsha, which becomes Xerxes in Greek. The Greek name Ἀσσουήρος (Assouéros) and then the Latin Vulgate (Assuetus) and the French Segond (Assuérus) preserve this root. In Hebrew, the word designates a monarch clothed with absolute authority over his provinces.
H0325.emploi: Ahasuerus appears 30 times in the Bible, almost entirely concentrated in the book of Esther (chapters 1 to 10), and twice in Ezra and Daniel. He is a known historical sovereign, which gives the narrative of Esther its grounding in the real history of Persia. The book of Esther does not hide his flaws: selfish, quick-tempered, prone to sign decrees without considering their consequences. Yet, it is through this king that divine providence saves the Jewish people. In Ezra 4:6, his name appears simply in a context of conflict. In Daniel 9:1, he is named Darius (likely a parallel tradition about a Persian king), which shows the complexity of Persian chronology in biblical sources.
H0325.portee: The narrative of Ahasuerus teaches that God governs even the hearts of the most powerful kings, without the king himself knowing it. Ahasuerus is unaware that his decisions serve God's purpose: his marriage to Esther, his growing favor for her, his sudden reversal against Haman—all converge to save the Jews. It is a call to trust in divine providence even when going through times of oppression under a hostile or indifferent authority.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H0326.detail: Ahashtari is a man from the tribe of Judah, mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 4:6. He is the son of Ashhur and Naarah, and the brother of Achuzzam, Hepher, and Themeni. He is part of the genealogies of Judah that trace the descendants of the ancient patriarchs.
H0326.origine: His name literally means "I will diligently observe the search." It is a typical Hebrew name of the time, composed of verbal elements that express an attitude or action. The name reflects the naming conventions of Judean families.
H0326.emploi: Ahashtari appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:6. He is listed among the children that Naarah bore to Ashhur, alongside his brothers Achuzzam, Hepher, and Themeni. His mention is part of the detailed genealogies of the tribe of Judah, which enumerate the families and their descendants during the divided monarchy.

sens: pack or saddle animal, resulting from a horse and a female donkey
fast and reliable royal mount
H0327.detail:
1. The mule is a hybrid animal born from the mating of a horse and a female donkey. More robust and enduring than the horse, stronger than the donkey, it was highly valued for carrying loads and serving as a mount, especially in difficult terrain. In Esther 8:10, it is mentioned among the animals used for royal couriers, alongside horses.
2. In the Persian empire, the mule becomes a symbol of royal speed and reliability. The king's couriers ride "horses and mules" (Esther 8:10 and 8:14) to quickly transport official orders; it is a mark of the power and authority of the sovereign to use such prestigious mounts.
H0327.origine: The Hebrew word אֲחַשְׁתְּרָן likely comes from Persian and specifically refers to this luxury mount used in the Persian empire. It is a borrowed word from the royal Persian context, highlighting the exoticism and prestige of these animals in the narrative of the book of Esther.
H0327.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Esther (8:10 and 8:14), during the account of the decree saving the Jews from persecution. In these two occurrences, the mule is depicted as the mount of royal couriers sent in haste to publish the king Ahasuerus's edict. The context emphasizes urgency, royal authority, and the prestige of these distinguished animals, worthy of the official messengers of the empire.
H0327.portee: The mule reminds the reader that God acts even through the structures of this world — here, the Persian empire — to accomplish His purpose of saving His people. These concrete details of ancient royal life show how divine providence manifests in ordinary events and the decisions of the powerful.

sens: One who claims to command spirits or occult powers
One who consults the dead or practices divination
Practitioner of magical arts or sorcery
H0328A.detail:
1. An enchanter is someone who claims to have supernatural power over spirits, genies, or hidden powers, and who boasts about it or uses it to impress others. In Isaiah 19:3, God promises that the enchanters of Egypt will be powerless against His judgment.
2. The term also refers to one who practices necromancy, that is, who claims to communicate with the dead or the spirits of the deceased to obtain revelations or advice.
3. More broadly, it is a practitioner of magical arts, a sorcerer who uses formulas, rituals, or invocations to produce supernatural effects — practices that the Law of Israel strictly prohibited.
H0328A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes a whisper, a murmur, or a dull sound — the image of magical formulas whispered, incantations spoken softly by which one claims to command spirits. This is why the old English translation was "mutterer" (one who murmurs). The word belongs to the family of occult practices strictly forbidden in Israel.
H0328A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 19:3. It is included in a list of occult practitioners — idols, enchanters, necromancers, diviners — that God will render mute and powerless during His judgment on Egypt. The context shows that these enchanters are seen as advisors to whom the people of Egypt turn, but who can do nothing against the will of the God of Israel.
H0328A.portee: This word reminds us that the temptation to consult spirits, to seek hidden secrets through occult means, has always existed — even among the most powerful kingdoms like Egypt. It warns that these practices are contrary to faith in God alone and that their supposed effectiveness is an illusion: only the living God holds true wisdom and control over the future.

sens: Slowly, without haste
Softly, without harshness or roughness
With moderate intensity, gradually
In speaking of an action, a word, or a current: in a calm and peaceful manner
H0328B.detail:
1. Slowly, without haste: the word describes a movement or progression that is slowed down. Jacob promises Esau to follow "slowly" at the pace of the flock and the children (Genesis 33:14), as he cannot move as quickly as his brother.
2. Softly, without harshness: it also indicates the absence of violence or roughness in action or treatment. The king asks that the young Absalom be treated "gently" (2 Samuel 18:5), meaning without being struck or killed.
3. With moderate intensity, gradually: the word can evoke a progressive or measured action. Ahab repents while walking "slowly," visible signs of a humble conversion (1 Kings 21:27).
4. In a calm and peaceful manner: to describe a word or a current that flows without agitation. The waters of Siloam flow "gently" (Isaiah 8:6), and the consolations of God are heard "gently" by those who receive them (Job 15:11).
H0328B.origine: The Hebrew word עַט (at) expresses the idea of delicacy, restraint, and absence of agitation. It likely comes from an ancient root that evokes slow and regulated movement. It is a simple yet rich word that appears rarely in the Hebrew Bible but always in contexts filled with emotion or spiritual meaning.
H0328B.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always translated into French as "gently" or "slowly." It characterizes very varied situations: a physical movement (Genesis 33:14, 1 Kings 21:27), an attitude of respect or restraint towards a person (2 Samuel 18:5), a natural flow or a teaching that is communicated smoothly (Isaiah 8:6, Job 15:11). In each case, the word emphasizes an action or state devoid of violence, haste, or agitation. It is a term chosen to express both prudence, meekness, and peace.
H0328B.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize the value of restraint, gentleness, and respect for the pace of others. The Bible does not only glorify speed or strength but also the ability to act with measure and kindness. It is a valuable lesson for those who wish to live in peace with God and with their fellow beings: there is wisdom in listening "gently" to the voice of God and treating others with the same delicacy.

sens: Location in the West Bank, west of the Jordan, between the Jordan and Jericho
Open space where grains were threshed to separate the grain from the chaff
H0329G.detail: 1. The proper name "Atad" designates a specific place in the West Bank, located between the Jordan and Jericho, on the west bank of the river. It is at this location that Jacob's funeral procession stopped: "They came to the threshing floor of Atad" (Genesis 50:10), where the family mourned greatly. 2. A threshing floor was an open, flat, and bare space where farmers would beat the ears of grain to detach the grain. The word thus evokes both a type of building or land and a common agricultural activity; this is likely why the place took this name: it resembled one of those common threshing floors. The Egyptian people who witnessed the mourning of the Hebrews in this place also called it "Abel-Mizraim," meaning "the mourning of the Egyptians" (Genesis 50:11).
H0329G.origine: The Hebrew word אָטָד (atad) literally means "threshing floor" or more broadly "area" (open and cleared space). It comes from the root that describes a flat and bare place used for agricultural work. The name was given to this location in the Jordan region due to its topography: a surface suitable for the threshing of grains, a common practice in the ancient Near East.
H0329G.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the account of Jacob's funeral in Genesis 50. It designates a specific geographical location where the funeral procession stopped: "They came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan" (Genesis 50:10). The Egyptians who accompanied Jacob mourned greatly at this place, which led the people of the land to call it "the mourning of the Egyptians" (Genesis 50:11). The threshing floor of Atad thus remains a significant point in patriarchal history, marked by respect and solemnity of mourning.
H0329G.portee: This place reminds us that the great events of life — particularly death and mourning — mark human geographies and enter into collective memory. The respect shown by the Egyptians for Israel's mourning illustrates how piety towards the dead transcends borders and cultures.

sens: Spiny shrub of little value
Image of a vain and threatening authority
H0329H.detail:
1. It is a small shrub covered with thorns, of little utility or beauty — barely good for firewood. This is what the important trees of Lebanon (the cedar) disdainfully mock (Judges 9:14-15).
2. It symbolizes hollow and dangerous power: the thorn bush pretends to reign and even threatens the noble trees with destructive fire (Judges 9:15), an image of a weak but malevolent leader who brings only ruin. In Psalm 58:10, the thorn represents what is worthless but irritating and is finally rejected.
H0329H.origine: The word designates a low, thorny Mediterranean shrub, probably the "buckthorn" (rhamnus). The root evokes the idea of pricking or wounding. It is a simple word that paints the concrete image of an insignificant yet prickly plant.
H0329H.emploi: The word appears 3 times in the Hebrew Bible. Its first two uses are found in Jotham's parable (Judges 9), where the trees seek a king and mock the thorn bush that unscrupulously accepts this charge — a caricature of Abimelech, a leader of little value and violent. The third use, in Psalm 58, uses the thorn to evoke what is despicable and is rejected. In all cases, the word paints a reality that is small, prickly, and threatening without true foundation.
H0329H.portee: This image of the thorn bush reminds us that power without wisdom or justice is vain and destructive. It invites us not to be impressed by the hollow threats of those who lack true moral weight, and to denounce the leader who abuses his authority to do harm.

sens: Fine filament of textile material intended to be woven or sewn
H0330.detail: 1. This word refers to thread in a material sense: the fine and strong filament obtained by twisting fibers (linen, wool, etc.) that is used to weave fabrics or sew. The word particularly evokes the linen thread of Egypt, known for its fineness and quality. The woman in Proverbs 7:16 prepares her bed with coverings adorned with these precious threads, symbolizing luxury and seduction.
H0330.origine: The Hebrew word אֵטוּן (étoun) designates linen transformed into thread, meaning the textile fiber ready for use. It is related to the cultivation of flax, which was very important in ancient Egypt, where this plant was massively cultivated to make fine and precious fabrics. The Egyptian context of the text ("Egyptian thread") shows that this term refers to a well-known commercial product in the ancient world.
H0330.emploi: This word appears only once in the Greek New Testament (translated from the Hebrew of the Old Testament). It is used in the context of luxury and seduction: Proverbs 7:16 mentions "Egyptian thread" as an element of the rich and tempting decor of the bed where the adulterous woman receives her lover. The use of the term emphasizes the refined quality and high cost of these coverings, thus marking the opulence and pride of seduction.
H0330.portee: This term reminds us how the temptations of sin are often wrapped in beauty and luxury. The text of Proverbs shows that sensual attraction also arises from material comfort and outward appearance. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation not to be seduced by the prestige of earthly things, even the most beautiful, and to remain vigilant against the allurements that can lead away from divine wisdom.

sens: Completely close, block, obstruct
Close the lips, silence
Close the ear, refuse to listen
H0331.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to close, to block an opening. In 1 Kings 6:4, the windows of the temple are "grated," meaning they are fitted with grates that partially close them; in Ezekiel 40:16, the same word describes "grated" windows in the chambers, with the same idea of partial or louvered closure.
2. Closing the lips means to keep silent. The one who "closes" his lips in Proverbs 17:28 is a wise man who does not speak lightly; it is a wisdom of restraint and discretion.
3. Closing the ear means deliberately refusing to listen, willfully ignoring. In Proverbs 21:13, the one who "closes" his ear to the cry of the poor acts with hardness of heart; in Isaiah 33:15, the one who "closes" his ear to bloodthirsty words consciously chooses not to hear evil and not to be corrupted by it. It is an act of moral will, sometimes culpable (indifference of the rich), sometimes virtuous (refusal of evil).
H0331.origine: The Hebrew verb אָטַם comes from a root that evokes the idea of closing, obstructing. It is used for both material objects (windows, doors) and for moral or physical actions (to be silent, to cease listening). The family of the word suggests the idea of a barrier that opposes passage or perception.
H0331.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, notably in Proverbs, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. It primarily describes the closure of architectural openings: grated windows of the temple (1 Kings 6:4; Ezekiel 40:16 and 41:16). But it also carries a moral and spiritual meaning: closing the lips through wisdom and restraint (Proverbs 17:28), or closing the ear through hardness of heart (Proverbs 21:13) or conversely through virtue (Isaiah 33:15). The context reveals whether the gesture is blameworthy or praiseworthy. In Psalms 58:5, the asp that "closes" its ear symbolizes the obstinate refusal of malice.
H0331.portee: This word teaches Christians two opposing wisdoms: on one hand, one must know how to "close" their lips and ears to what corrupts, to evil words and temptations (Isaiah 33:15); on the other hand, one must guard against "closing" their heart to the misery of others (Proverbs 21:13). True wisdom discerns what is appropriate to listen to and what must be rejected, rather than closing oneself off out of pride or indifference.

sens: Close, shut
Close the mouth, be silent
Enclose, imprison
H0332.detail:
1. To close or shut something, like closing a door or a lid: it is to block access, the opening. In Psalms 69:16, the psalmist begs God that "the pit does not close over me," meaning that he is not engulfed in death, as if it were closing over him.
2. Closing one's mouth means to be silent, to stop speaking. It is the image of lips closing and speech interrupting.
3. To close in on someone means to enclose them, imprison them, trap them. The word evokes the idea of being held, blocked, with no escape.
H0332.origine: The Hebrew verb אָטַר comes from a root that expresses the idea of closing, shutting, blocking. It is related to verbs that denote actions of closure or restriction. The basic image is that of a barrier, a limit set to prevent access or exit.
H0332.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 69:16. In this context of supplication, the psalmist fears being engulfed by the waters and that the pit — death — will close over him. The usage is clearly negative: it expresses the anguish of perishing, of losing all hope of escaping danger. The word belongs to the dramatic vocabulary of lamentations.
H0332.portee: This verse reminds the believer that in times of extreme distress — when everything seems to overwhelm us and we risk sinking — it is right to cry out to God. The psalmist does not resign himself to misfortune: he pleads that God does not leave him "enclosed" in death. It is a lesson in trust and persistence in prayer, even in the midst of the worst trials.

sens: A man from the family of Hezekiah during the time of exile and return
A family leader whose descendants return from captivity
H0333G.detail: Ather is a figure from the time of exile and return to Jerusalem. He appears as a family leader: his sons — numbering ninety-eight — are among those who return from Babylonian captivity (Ezra 2:16). Ather was related to Hezekiah, suggesting a prestigious lineage, although he himself remained in exile. His name, which means "the one who binds" or "binder," may reflect a role or quality of one who maintains unity. The same data reappears in Nehemiah 7:21, where the list of exiles returned is repeated, showing the importance of this genealogy for the reconstruction of Israel.
H0333G.origine: The name Ather literally means "the one who binds" or "who attaches," derived from a root evoking the action of binding together. This etymology fits well with a family leader — one who "binds" or gathers his own — and illustrates how Hebrew names often reflect a quality or function. The name appears exclusively in the lists of the return from exile.
H0333G.emploi: Ather is mentioned exactly twice, in two parallel passages: Ezra 2:16 and Nehemiah 7:21. These two verses report the enumeration of families returning from Babylonian captivity. In both cases, Ather is presented as the head of a lineage of ninety-eight people, belonging to the family of Hezekiah. This repetition underscores the importance of preserving and transmitting genealogies at the time of return, to attest to the identity and rights of each in the reclaimed Promised Land. Ather himself does not appear among the returnees, but his descendants carry his name and legacy.
H0333G.portee: The name of Ather reminds us that even minor figures in biblical history play a role in God's plan. Although few details are given, his presence in the genealogical records shows that God knows and counts each of His children. For the returning exiles, the ability to preserve and claim their lineage is an act of hope and faith in the promise of return.

sens: Family of temple porters during the time of Exile and return
Descendants of an ancestor bearing this name
H0333H.detail: Ather is the name of a Levitical family of porters (gatekeepers) of the Temple in Jerusalem. In Ezra 2:42, they are listed among the porters who returned from exile in Babylon: "the sons of Ather" form a group from this priestly class. The same group appears in Nehemiah 7:45, in a parallel list of the return, confirming that this family played a stable role in the worship of the restored Temple after the exile.
H0333H.origine: The name Ather comes from the Hebrew root אתר (atar), which means "to bind" or "to attach." This image evokes the role of one who "binds" or "holds closed" — appropriate for a porter who guards and closes the doors of the sanctuary. It is a name of function as well as family descent.
H0333H.emploi: Ather appears twice in the Bible, always as an ancestor of a family of porters. In Ezra 2:42, during the return of the exiles under Zerubbabel, the "sons of Ather" are counted among a total of one hundred thirty-nine porters. The same list is repeated in Nehemiah 7:45, with a slightly lower total (one hundred thirty-eight), which likely reflects variations in generations. These two passages show that this Levitical family maintained its charge as gatekeepers of the restored Temple.

sens: Leader of Israel during the time of Nehemiah
H0333I.detail: Ather is an Israelite leader who sealed the covenant of Nehemiah at the time of the return from exile to Jerusalem. He is among the signatories of the solemn document mentioned in Nehemiah 10:17, alongside other leaders of the people.
H0333I.origine: The Hebrew name אָטֵר (ater) literally means "the one who binds" or "the one who binds firmly," derived from a root evoking the idea of tying, tightening. This meaning fits well with the role of a leader who engages the people through a covenant.
H0333I.emploi: Ather appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:17. He is mentioned among the leaders and elders of Israel who solemnly signed the covenant document that Nehemiah established after the return from Babylonian exile. This list shows the main religious and civil leaders of the reconstituted community of Jerusalem.

sens: One who cannot or does not use the right hand
One who has a stronger or more skillful left hand than the right hand
H0334.detail:
1. The word literally describes a person whose right hand is "bound," meaning non-functional or unusable. This is the case of Ehud, the deliverer of Israel sent by God against the king of Moab: he did not "use the right hand" (Judges 3:15), which may have made him an invalid, or at least someone unusual in the eyes of his enemies.
2. By extension, the term applies to those who naturally use their left hand skillfully, such as the slingers from the tribe of Benjamin, who "did not use the right hand" and could "aim at a hair without missing" (Judges 20:16). Here, the "bound right hand" is a physical peculiarity or a strategic choice that does not hinder effectiveness; quite the opposite.
H0334.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of being bound, closed, hindered — the right hand is, so to speak, "closed" or inactive. The word literally translates the inability or absence of use of the dominant hand in most people (the right). It is a concrete physical description, without moral connotation.
H0334.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Old Testament, both in the book of Judges. In each case, it designates a particular characteristic: first, the judge Ehud, a man chosen by God to deliver Israel despite (or perhaps because of) this peculiarity; then an elite group of Benjaminites, exceptional warriors who turned this difference into a martial advantage. The biblical usage suggests that this condition was rare and remarkable, unusual enough to be mentioned as a distinctive trait.
H0334.portee: These accounts show that God does not choose His deliverers based on "normal" human strength: He uses atypical men, even those considered disabled in the eyes of the world, to accomplish His purposes. "Weakness" or physical difference never disqualifies someone from serving God; it can even become the occasion for His power to manifest.

sens: Interrogative adverb asking for place, location
Interrogative adverb asking for direction, origin
Interrogative adverb asking for state or condition
Exclamatory adverb expressing absence or enigma
With another adverb, reinforces or specifies the question
H0335.detail:
1. "Where" inquires about the place: "Where are you?" asks in which location the person is (Genesis 3:9). This is the most direct and common question.
2. "Where" can also ask about provenance or direction: "Where are you?" can mean "where do you come from?" or "where are you going?" (1 Samuel 9:18: "where is the house of the seer?").
3. The word serves to ask about fate, state, or condition: "Where are your gods now?" (Deuteronomy 32:37) asks not for the location, but what has become of them.
4. Used exclamatively, "where" expresses enigma or absence: "Where is the way to the dwelling of light?" (Job 38:19) — this is a rhetorical question showing inaccessibility.
5. In combination with other adverbs, "where" reinforces or specifies: "from which city are you?" (2 Samuel 15:2) combines place and quality.
H0335.origine: This interrogative adverb comes from the Hebrew root "ay" which carries the fundamental idea of questioning about place or location. It is related to simple interrogative forms common in Semitic languages. The word is purely interrogative: it serves to ask a question, without carrying a response or affirmation within itself.
H0335.emploi: This adverb appears 37 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives (Samuel, Kings), wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes), and the prophets. It is the classic tool for asking where someone or something is: God questions Adam "Where are you?" after his fall (Genesis 3:9), Cain is confronted with "Where is your brother?" (Genesis 4:9). In dialogues with God or His servants, "where" seeks a location or state. In the prophets like Job and Isaiah, the word often serves to pose deeper questions that challenge or express the enigma of the world: Job asks "Where are the riches?" (Job 20:7), Isaiah asks "Where is the certificate of divorce?" (Isaiah 50:1).
H0335.portee: For the reader, "where" is the primary question that God poses to sinful man: it invites awareness of his state and position before God. It is also the human inquiry in the face of the divine mystery — Job and the wise ask "where?" to acknowledge the inaccessibility of certain realities. This simple question reminds us that we inhabit a spatial world and that God knows exactly where we are.

sens: one who has committed a fault, a crime, or a sin
person judged responsible for a transgression
H0336.detail: 1. The word designates one who has committed a fault or sin and bears the guilt. In Job 22:30, Eliphaz asserts that God will deliver "the guilty," meaning one who is burdened with faults, through the intercession of a righteous person: the guilty here is not without hope, for the purity of an innocent's hands can obtain his deliverance.
H0336.origine: This Hebrew word belongs to the family of words expressing guilt and responsibility in transgression. It is formed from a root that emphasizes the link between the fault committed and the one who bears it. In biblical context, the notion of guilt is inseparable from that of responsibility before God.
H0336.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 22:30. Eliphaz uses it in a speech intended to convince Job that his personal righteousness can obtain deliverance for others, even for one who bears the weight of his own sins. This passage highlights the doctrine of intercession: the guilty, as burdened as he may be with his faults, is not abandoned if a righteous person intercedes for him.
H0336.portee: This verse teaches a profound truth: no sinner is beyond the reach of God's grace, especially when others intercede for him. For the Christian, this image foreshadows the role of intercession and the power of Christ's righteousness to justify us before God. It also invites us not to despair for those who have sinned, but to intercede for them.

sens: Exclamation expressing compassion before a dire fate
Warning directed against one who is in danger
H0337.detail:
1. The word is an interjection — an exclamation that bursts forth from the lips to express a feeling. Here, it is the feeling of compassion: one sees someone in a difficult situation and exclaims "woe!" as one would say "what a pity!" In Ecclesiastes 4:10, the wise man sees a man alone who falls without anyone to lift him up, and he exclaims "woe to him who is alone!" — the exclamation underscores how pitiful this solitude is.
2. Sometimes the word takes on a tone of warning: it designates a misfortune that threatens and that one would want to avoid. In Ecclesiastes 10:16, "Woe to you, land" warns the people against the consequences of poor governance — it is almost a prophecy of what will happen if caution is not taken.
H0337.origine: This Hebrew interjection directly expresses an emotion in the face of misfortune — as if it were a cry from the heart. It belongs to the family of exclamations that burst forth in everyone's speech, without any particular grammatical construction. It is one of the many interjections that Hebrew uses to convey feelings: piety, pain, surprise, warning.
H0337.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Ecclesiastes — the book of practical wisdom. In both cases, the wise man uses the exclamation to highlight a dire fate: the solitude of one who has no one to help him, and the consequences of chaotic governance. It is a word of spoken language that the writer uses to give weight to his moral warning.
H0337.portee: This interjection shows us that the Bible recognizes and expresses the misfortunes of life with simplicity and emotion.
