H0367.emploi: This word appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic books (Job, Psalms) and in historical narratives (Genesis, Exodus, Joshua). It designates either the terror that God sends or that emanates from Him, or the fear that a man feels in the face of the divine or the powerful, or the fear that seizes a people. In the stories, terror is often a divine weapon that subdues the enemies of Israel (Exodus 23:27, Joshua 2:9). In the poems of Job, it becomes the expression of existential anxiety and human suffering before the mysteries of God. It can also be what accompanies divine revelation or the experience of the numinous.
H0367.portee: This word reminds us that fear is not always a weakness: it can be a rightful reaction before the holiness and power of God. Understanding that God sends His terror before Israel shows that the fear of God is a spiritual weapon that protects His people. But the terror that overwhelms Job also teaches that the believer can go through nights of anxiety and dread, and that this too is part of the journey of faith.

sens: Ancient giant people who inhabited the region of Moab before the Moabites
Name given by the Moabites to these giants
The "terrors" or fearsome creatures of the Promised Land
H0368.detail:
1. The Emim were an ancient and powerful people who occupied the region of Moab before the Moabites settled there. The Bible mentions them as a population of great size, comparable to the Anakim and the Rephaim, those feared giants of Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:10). Kedorlaomer and his allies fought against them in the time of Abraham (Genesis 14:5).

2. The Moabites themselves called these ancient inhabitants the "Emim," which literally means "terrors" or "fearsome creatures" — a name that reflects the fear and respect inspired by these giants (Deuteronomy 2:11). It was their way of designating these vanished peoples of whom only the memory remained.
H0368.origine: The name "Emim" comes from a Hebrew root meaning "terror" or "fright." This evocative name captures the impression left by these giants: impressive and feared creatures. In Hebrew, the word recalls the dread inspired by these vanished peoples. The name is preserved in the Bible to show how ancient peoples understood the former inhabitants of the Promised Land as formidable and legendary beings.
H0368.emploi: The Emim are mentioned three times in the Bible, only in the Pentateuch. First in Genesis 14:5, where Kedorlaomer defeats them militarily, alongside other giant peoples like the Rephaim. Then in Deuteronomy 2:10-11, Moses reminds the Israelites that the Emim once inhabited the region of Moab, as a great, numerous, and tall people, before being replaced by the Moabites. The Bible systematically classifies them among the peoples of giants, of the same order as the Rephaim and the Anakim. Their repeated mention serves to remind that God had powerful peoples to drive out before Israel.
H0368.portee: The Emim symbolize the seemingly insurmountable obstacles that God asks His people to overcome. Although terrifying in their size and strength, these giants did not withstand the God of Israel, who drove them out of the Promised Land. For the Christian reader, their example teaches that obstacles — even the most intimidating — cannot resist Him who leads His people. It is a call to trust in God rather than in our own strength.

sens: The total absence of something
The non-existence of a person or thing
The absence of value or importance
That which is vain or without substance
H0369.detail:
1. Nothingness refers to absolute emptiness, that which does not exist at all. When Isaiah 40:23 says that God brings princes to "nothingness," it means they become as if they do not exist, annihilated by His power.

2. In human relationships, it is the absence of a person. Genesis 40:8: Joseph tells the servants that "no one" can interpret their dreams, meaning that no man possesses that power. Similarly, 1 Samuel 14:17: Saul observes that Jonathan and his armor-bearer are "missing" from the assembly.

3. The word also expresses the absence of help or support. Psalms 142:5: the psalmist cries that "no one" recognizes him and that "no one" cares for his soul — he feels terribly alone, abandoned by all.

4. It can signify the absence of intrinsic value. When Jeremiah 30:17 speaks of Zion as a "castaway that no one cares for," the word refers to what is rejected, lacking importance in the eyes of men.
H0369.origine: The Hebrew word אַיִן (ayin) comes from a root expressing absence or emptiness. It is fundamentally a negation: it states what is not, what is lacking. The word is used as an adjective, adverb, or noun depending on the context. In Greek, it corresponds to absence, nothingness, non-existence.
H0369.emploi: This word is among the most frequent in the Bible (687 occurrences). It appears in all books, from the Pentateuch to the New Testament translated into Hebrew. It can mean "there is no one" (Genesis 40:8; Job 1:8), "there is nothing" (Genesis 2:5, where no plant exists yet), or "it is vain, without value" (Isaiah 40:23). The context determines its nuance: material deprivation, absence of a person, lack of support, or negation of a quality. The Bible also uses it to express the absence of fear of God (Genesis 20:11) or the absence of reproaches (Genesis 39:9).
H0369.portee: This word reminds the reader that only God is truly real, that everything that exists outside of Him can become nothingness. It also invites us to recognize when we ourselves are in need or absence, and to seek our help in God rather than in human powers that are only "nothingness." It humbles us in the face of our fragility.

sens: From what place, from which location?
From which place?
To what place?
From what source, from what origin?
H0370.detail:
1. The word asks for the identification of the place where someone or something is located. Jacob asks the shepherds: "Where are you from?" to know their region of origin (Genesis 29:4). It is the simplest and most direct question.
2. Sometimes it specifically marks the point of departure, the place from which one comes. Satan answers God: "Where do you come from?" — meaning where are you arriving from? (Job 1:7). The word then emphasizes the journey taken.
3. In some cases, it can point to the destination or direction: "Where are you going?" asks the old man to the traveler (Judges 19:17). The context then indicates the movement towards a place.
4. Rarely, it extends to the figurative sense of source or non-geographical origin. When Elisha asks, "With what shall I save you?" (2 Kings 6:27), the word refers to the source or means available.
H0370.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of place or position. It is a primitive interrogative particle, among the oldest grammatical tools in Hebrew. It belongs to the same family as other words of place and direction, and it poses an open question about space or origin.
H0370.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in narratives and dialogues. It is found in Genesis (Jacob questioning the shepherds about their region), in the historical books (Joshua, Judges, Kings) where it introduces conversations, and in the poetic and prophetic books (Job, Psalms, Isaiah) where it often carries a more serious or theological weight. In Job 1:7, God asks Satan where he comes from, a question that reveals the wandering nature of evil. The meaning remains stable: it is always an inquiry about place or origin.
H0370.portee: This small word reminds us that our origins, our affiliations, and our backgrounds matter in the biblical narrative. The questions "Where do you come from?" and "Where are you going?" are at the heart of the life of faith: they invite transparency, self-knowledge, and the expectation of salvation. When God asks Satan where he comes from, this question reveals that no one escapes divine inquiry: everything is known to the Lord.

sens: Direct question particle expecting an affirmative answer
Rhetorical question: call to confirm what seems obvious
H0371.detail:
1. This Hebrew particle introduces a direct question — here "Do you not have a spear or a sword at hand?" (1 Samuel 21:8) — assuming that the answer will be "yes." David asks Ahimelech to confirm the presence of a weapon, framing the question in a way that presupposes one exists.
2. It is a rhetorical inquiry, which seeks less information than to prompt the interlocutor to agree: the questioner asserts while questioning. This turn of phrase is lively and pressing, especially in an urgent situation like that of David, who needs a sword and asks for it insistently.
H0371.origine: This particle belongs to the class of Hebrew interrogative words. It expresses absence or negation while posing the question: hence its form "n'", which captures this interrogative-negative nuance in French. It is a very ancient grammatical tool in Semitic languages to mark the expectation of a positive response.
H0371.emploi: The word appears only once in 1 Samuel 21:8, where David questions Ahimelech the priest. It is a moment of urgency: David is fleeing, pursued by Saul, and he has lost his weapons. The question, framed with this particle, concerns the presence of a weapon available to the priest. The tone is direct and pressing, suited to the gravity of the situation.
H0371.portee: This particle shows how the Bible reports the authentic words of men in their critical moments. It invites the reader to feel the urgency and intensity of the prayer or request: it is a literary tool that brings the scene to life rather than recounting it from a distance.

sens: Son of Gilead, himself the son of Manasseh
Eponymous ancestor of the clan of the Jazerites
H0372.detail:
1. Jazer is a man from the tribe of Manasseh, son of Gilead. He lived during the time of Egypt and the desert, and appears in the genealogy of Manasseh alongside his brothers Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Shemida, and Hepher (Numbers 26:30).
2. His name gives rise to the clan of the Jazerites, one of the family groups of Manasseh listed during the census in the desert. The descendants of Jazer bear his name and thus form an identified lineage within the tribal structure of Israel.
H0372.origine: The name Jazer literally means "no help" or "without aid," composed of a negation and a word denoting help. It is a typical Hebrew name from the patriarchal and desert period. The same name, with an additional element, is found in Abiezer (Abijézer), which means "my father is help," thus forming an interesting semantic contrast within the same family.
H0372.emploi: Jazer appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogical list of Numbers 26:30, during the second census of Israel in the desert. He is mentioned as a son of Gilead and ancestor of the Jazerites, one of the clans of the tribe of Manasseh. His appearance in this administrative and genealogical context underscores his role as a founding figure of an Israelite family, even though his personal life is not recounted in detail in the Scriptures.

sens: person descending from Iezer, a man of the tribe of Manasseh
H0373.detail: 1. The Jezerites are the members of the clan or family descending from Iezer, a man of the tribe of Manasseh. This term specifically refers to the descendants of Iezer at the time of the census of the Hebrew people in the desert, after the exodus from Egypt. In Numbers 26:30, during the great census of the Israelites, Moses lists the different families of Gilead (the father of Iezer) and mentions the Jezerites as one of the branches of this lineage.
H0373.origine: The word comes from Iezer (אִיעֶזֶר), a family leader of the tribe of Manasseh, son of Gilead. The suffix "-ites" or "-rites" (in Hebrew -י) is common for forming names of peoples or clans from an ancestor: it means "the descendants of" or "the family of." Iezer himself has a name meaning "God helps" or "my father helps."
H0373.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:30. It is found in the context of the second census of the people of Israel in the desert, after leaving Egypt and before entering Canaan. Moses methodically lists all the families from the twelve tribes, giving for each the name of the founding ancestor and the name of the clan that descends from it. The Jezerites take their place in this solemn genealogical list alongside other families of Manasseh such as the Helekites, the Asrielites, the Shechemites, and the Apherites.
H0373.portee: This verse shows us how God knows each family of Israel by name, each branch of His people. It reminds us that divine Providence cares about genealogies and family ties, and that every lineage matters in the history of salvation. It is also a testimony to God's faithfulness to the promises made to Abraham: He has indeed multiplied his descendants into many families and clans.

sens: Unit of measurement for dry goods (grains, flour)
Container intended to hold or measure this quantity
Standard quantity used in religious offerings and commercial transactions
H0374.detail:
1. The ephah is a unit of measurement for grains and flours, equivalent to three seahs or ten omers. Gideon uses an ephah of flour to make unleavened bread (Judges 6:19), and Ruth gathers about an ephah of barley from her work in the fields (Ruth 2:17). This measure represents approximately 40 liters.
2. The word also refers to the container itself, the basket or vessel that holds this quantity and is used for measuring. Zechariah sees in a vision a woman sitting inside an ephah (Zechariah 5:7), which shows that it was a sufficiently large container.
3. In temple offerings, the ephah becomes a standard measure: a tenth of an ephah of barley flour for the jealousy offering (Numbers 5:15), an ephah for each animal during the solemn feasts (Ezekiel 46:11). It is also a measure that must not be falsified: having two kinds of ephah (one for giving, the other for receiving) is an abomination in the eyes of the Lord (Proverbs 20:10).
H0374.origine: The word ephah comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to measure." It refers both to the action of measuring and the measuring instrument. In Hebrew, the same root appears in other words related to quantification. This measure was a central element of the economic and religious life of Israel, used for grain trade, taxes, and offerings at the sanctuary.
H0374.emploi: The word ephah appears 29 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the books of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) where it sets the quantities of offerings, but also in narratives (Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel) and among the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Micah, Zechariah). In the Law, the ephah measures portions of flour, oil, and grain offered to the Lord: a tenth of an ephah of flour in certain sacrifices (Leviticus 5:11, Numbers 28:5). In narratives, it simply measures the grain or flour used for cooking (Judges 6:19). Among the prophets, the ephah becomes a symbol: Amos criticizes those who reduce the ephah to cheat (Amos 8:5), and Zechariah transforms it into an apocalyptic vision (Zechariah 5). The emphasis on the correct measure (not two different ephahs) shows that commercial honesty is a central value in Israel.
H0374.portee: The ephah reminds us that God orders ordinary life — work, commerce, meals — according to principles of justice and measurement. The precise offerings at the sanctuary teach that our service to God is not vague sentiment, but concrete obedience in the details. The warning against the falsified ephah (Proverbs 20:10) shows that God sees and disapproves of dishonesty in the small things of commerce: there is no minor sin when it comes to justice. For the Christian, this invites faithfulness in the ordinary and in daily transactions.

sens: In what place, in what location
To what place, in what direction
With whom, near whom
What kind of, of what sort
H0375.detail:
1. "Where" asks for the precise location of a person or thing: "Where are Samuel and David?" asks Saul of those who know (1 Samuel 19:22). It is the simplest question, one that localizes.
2. "Where" can also ask to what place one is going, in what direction: "Where have you gleaned today?" asks Naomi of Ruth, trying to find out where she worked (Ruth 2:19).
3. "Where" is sometimes used to ask "with whom" or "near whom": "Where is he?" asks the king about Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:4), and the answer is a person, Machir.
4. More rarely, "where" takes the meaning of "what kind of" or "of what sort": "How were the men you killed?" asks Gideon (Judges 8:18), where "how" translates the same Hebrew word, questioning the nature or appearance rather than the location.
H0375.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of place or location. It is an interrogative adverb, formed to pose a question. In Hebrew, it is one of the elementary questions: to search for a person, find a thing, or understand the nature of a situation, one begins by asking "where." The word is very ancient in the language, reflecting the primary needs of human communication.
H0375.emploi: This word appears about 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the narrative accounts of Genesis, Judges, Samuel, and in biblical wisdom literature like Job. It is always a direct question, never an assertion. In Genesis, Joseph seeks his brothers and asks "where" they are pasturing their flock (Genesis 37:16). In 1 Samuel, Saul questions people to locate Samuel and David (1 Samuel 19:22). The meaning of "where" is dominant, but in a few cases, particularly in Job, it shifts to "what" or "how," questioning quality or nature rather than position (Job 4:7: "What are the just who have been exterminated?"). It is thus a flexible question, suited to various contexts.
H0375.portee: For the reader, this simple question "where" reminds us that searching and locating are at the heart of many biblical narratives: we seek God, we seek our path, we seek justice. The question "where" opens dialogue, exposes need, and often prepares a response that changes everything. It also invites reflection: where am I in my walk with God? Where is my trust placed?

sens: Human being of male sex, adult or child, male individual
Husband, spouse in the context of marriage
Human being in general, person (as opposed to God)
Servant, assistant, soldier in the service of a master
Remarkable man, person of value or power
Any, each (in a distributive sense)
H0376G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a man in the physical and biological sense: a male human, distinct from a woman. Genesis 2:23 illustrates this perfectly: Adam sees the woman created from him and says, "she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man" — he refers to himself as the one from whom the woman is derived.
2. By natural extension, it designates the husband in the marital relationship: the man who takes a woman as a wife and forms a unit with her. Genesis 2:24 speaks of the bond between the man and his wife in marriage.
3. The word broadens to designate any human being, any person, emphasizing our created and mortal nature before God. Proverbs 16:27 speaks of "the wicked man" in a broad sense: any human capable of good or evil.
4. It also designates a man in the sense of servant or soldier: one who obeys a master and carries out his orders. In 2 Kings 10:24, Jehu places "eighty men" to accomplish a specific mission.
5. Sometimes the word elevates dignity: it designates a remarkable, powerful, or wise man. Genesis 41:38 speaks of Joseph as a man in whom "the spirit of God" dwells — a spiritual greatness.
6. In a distributive context, it means "each," "any": Numbers 9:10 says "if any one of you" (literally "if a man"), to indicate a rule applicable to all.
H0376G.origine: The word אִישׁ comes from an ancient root designating the male human being and autonomy. It is related to Hebrew words expressing virility and responsibility. The implicit contrast in the biblical text is often with אִשָּׁה (woman): together, these two words express the duality of humanity as created. The Hebrew word אִישׁ embodies the idea of one who acts, decides, assumes a charge — the parent of the Hebrew איש (which also means "each") reflects this autonomy.
H0376G.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament (over 900 occurrences), present in all historical books, the Psalms, and wisdom literature. It primarily designates man in the literal sense: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their descendants are called "men." But it quickly extends: a man can be "great" or "wicked," servant or king, husband or warrior. In the Law (Exodus), the word appears to state rules concerning each individual or categories (a man who injures, a man who steals). In historical narratives (Samuel, Kings), it distinguishes men from women, marks the status or moral value of a person (2 Samuel 12:5: "the man who has done this deserves to die"). The word can also be used collectively or generally: "every man" or "any man." An important nuance: unlike the Greek anthropos which designates humanity in general, אִישׁ emphasizes man as a responsible individual and actor.
H0376G.portee: This word reminds the reader that man — each person — is created in the image of God, but also distinct from God and dependent on Him. It underscores personal responsibility: one is not an anonymous crowd, but an individual to whom God speaks and who must give account. In marriage, it establishes equality and complementarity: man and woman complete each other. Finally, it invites the reader to recognize themselves in this word: each believer is this "man" to whom the Word speaks and who must, like Abraham or David, seek to live according to divine will.

sens: the man to whom a woman is united by marriage
the spouse of a woman, to whom she must obey
the owner of a house, the head of the family
H0376H.detail:
1. The husband is the man married to a woman. He is the spouse, the one who shares the marital life. Genesis 3:6 clearly shows this: Eve gives the fruit to her husband Adam, who was with her.
2. In the laws of Israel, the husband is the head of the household and the one who validates or annuls his wife's vows. Numbers 30:12 and 30:15 explain that the commitments of a married woman depend on her husband's knowledge and approval.
3. The husband is responsible for supporting and protecting his wife. In Hosea 2:18, God promises to be for Israel like a faithful husband, suggesting that the husband is one who provides and commits long-term.
H0376H.origine: The Hebrew word ish (אִישׁ) is an ancient and fundamental term for designating the married man. Its root evokes the idea of strength and presence. The word contrasts with "woman" (isha), which shares its etymology. In biblical language, ish can also simply designate man in a general sense, but here it primarily carries the conjugal and domestic meaning.
H0376H.emploi: The word ish appears 65 times in the recorded biblical usages. It is heavily used in family narratives (Genesis, Ruth, 1 Samuel) and in the laws of marriage and vows (Numbers 30, Leviticus 21-22). Its usage shows that the husband is the one who recognizes the woman (Genesis 16:3), who remains with her (Genesis 3:6), who can forbid or approve her vows (Numbers 30), and who is bound to her by a covenant. In Hosea, the image of the husband becomes a metaphor for God as the husband of Israel, revealing the depth of this bond.
H0376H.portee: The word "husband" helps the reader understand that biblical marriage is not an equal contract, but a covenant where the husband bears authority and responsibility. It is a reminder that God presents Himself as the husband of Israel, which illuminates all the prophetic language of the Old Testament. For the believer, it is an invitation to reflect on the nature of marital commitment and the mystery of the covenant.

sens: Adult male of the human species, as opposed to woman
Husband, spouse in a marital relationship
Human being, any person (man or woman)
Servant, man in the service of a master
Each, every man indiscriminately
Man of value, warrior or prominent figure
H0376I.detail:
1. The man is primarily the adult male of humanity: this is the most basic meaning of the word. In Genesis 9:5, God says, "I will require the life of man from man" referring to a person who has shed the blood of another human being.
2. The word also designates the husband in marriage. It is the man as he forms a couple with his wife, one who has a particular responsibility in the household.
3. More broadly, it can mean any human being, man or woman. In Jeremiah 35:15, the Lord says, "Return each one from your evil way": the word applies to all without distinction of sex.
4. The man can also be a servant or a dependent of a master. In Exodus 12:44, the text speaks of a servant bought for money who participates in the Passover: he is a man under authority.
5. "Each one" expresses universality: in 1 Kings 22:17, the prophet sees Israel scattered and each returning "in peace to his house" — the idea is that every man will go his own way.
6. A man can also be a person of value or a notable warrior, like a champion. In Proverbs 27:17, "one man stirs up the anger of another man": two strong beings confronting each other.
H0376I.origine: The Hebrew word ish comes from a very ancient root that primarily designates the male human by his virility and strength. Words of the same family are found in other Semitic languages with the same meaning. The root evokes the idea of existence and personality — one who is present, who acts, who matters. Ish stands in opposition to several words: to "woman" (isha in Hebrew, the woman), to "God" (showing that man is created and dependent), and sometimes to "child" (one who is still growing).
H0376I.emploi: This word is one of the most common in the Old Testament: 499 occurrences in total. It appears in every book, from Genesis to Malachi, as speaking of human beings is inevitable. In Genesis, ish designates the men of the lineage of Adam and the patriarchs: Jacob, Joseph, etc. In Exodus and Leviticus, it applies to every member of the people of Israel, especially in laws concerning "every man" (like the tithe or the Sabbath). The word gradually expands: it can simply mean "someone" when one's identity is unknown, or conversely a particularly notable man. In Judges 4:20, "Is there anyone here?" shows this flexibility: the word means "any person." The translation varies greatly — "man," "each one," "person," "someone" — depending on the context, as the Hebrew word covers all these meanings.
H0376I.portee: For the Christian reader, ish reminds us that every person counts in the eyes of God, whether man or woman, servant or master, unknown or famous. It is a word that humanizes: it states that God cares for each one. When the Lord says, "I will require the life of man," He affirms the dignity and responsibility of each person before Him. The word also shows that in God's plan, all humanity — taken as a whole of individuals — is concerned by His covenant and justice.

sens: To show oneself worthy of the role of man, to behave with virility and responsibility
To act with strength and assurance, to show character and determination
To stand with courage in the face of challenges
H0377.detail:
1. This verb calls the listener to remember his identity as a man and to fully live out its responsibilities. In Isaiah 46:8, the prophet exhorts sinners to "be men" — that is, to awaken their conscience, to shake off forgetfulness and negligence, and to conduct themselves with the maturity and dignity that the state of being a man requires.
2. The word carries the idea of strength, moral virility, and determination: to stand firm with character, to face reality without fleeing, and to act as a responsible person rather than as a passive or dazed child.
3. It is a call to cease behaving as a slave to one's passions or in foolish rebellion: to truly become a man is to take hold of oneself and return to oneself, as the prophetic context commands.
H0377.origine: This verb comes from the root ish (אִישׁ), which means "man" — not just the biological male, but the man in his fullness, his responsibility, and his strength. The form used here (Hithpael) gives the word a reflexive force: it is less an external command than a call to show oneself, to act in accordance with one's nature and dignity as a man. It is a powerful rhetorical resource: the prophet does not say "be afraid" or "obey," but "be what you truly are."
H0377.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 46:8. The prophet addresses Judah in exile, to a people who have lost their memory and courage, who have forgotten the acts of God. The call to "be a man" — to wake up, to reflect, to regain oneself — contrasts with the situation of those paralyzed by doubt and idolatry. It is a rare verb, used only once, which underscores the intensity of the prophetic message.
H0377.portee: This word resonates with the Christian in his struggle between flesh and spirit. To be a man in the biblical sense is to refuse cowardice, to cultivate spiritual virility — not arrogance or brutality, but a peaceful strength, a determination to live according to the truth and to be accountable for one's actions before God. It is a call to Christian maturity: to grow, to shake oneself, to take one's life in hand rather than to be dominated by fear or sin.

sens: Son of Saul, king of Israel for seven years
Brother of Jonathan and Michal
King in competition with David after Saul's death
H0378.detail: Ish-Bosheth is the son of Saul, the first king of Israel. After Saul's death at the battle of Gilboa, Abner, the general of the army, proclaims him king at Mahanaim and supports him militarily against David for seven years (2 Samuel 2:8-10). His name means "man of shame" in Hebrew, which reflects his weakened role: he is king of Israel but only truly reigns for two years, while David reigns over Judah (2 Samuel 2:10). Abner treats him with little respect, and when Ish-Bosheth dares to criticize him over a woman, Abner becomes angry and moves closer to David (2 Samuel 3:8). Ultimately, after Abner's assassination, Ish-Bosheth himself is killed by murderers who think to win David's favor, marking the end of Saul's house and the unification of the kingdom under David.
H0378.origine: His Hebrew name אִישׁ־בֹשֶׁת (ish-boshet) literally means "man" (ish) and "shame" (boshet). He is also called Eshbaal (אֶשְׁבַּעַל), which means "man of Baal," the Canaanite god. The biblical writers likely replaced "Baal" with "boshet" (shame) to show their disdain for this weak and illegitimate king in God's eyes. His name thus reveals the judgment on his reign: a reign marked by weakness and disgrace.
H0378.emploi: Ish-Bosheth appears ten times in the second book of Samuel, entirely in the story of his parallel reign with David (2 Samuel 2-4). The early mentions show him proclaimed king by Abner and leading an army against David (2 Samuel 2:8, 2:10, 2:12, 2:15). His interactions with Abner gradually reveal his incompetence: he can only receive orders, and when he dares to reproach something to his general, Abner gets angry and considers going to David (2 Samuel 3:8). David seeks to negotiate his marriage to Michal to strengthen his legitimacy (2 Samuel 3:14). The narrative ends with his assassination at Mahanaim, an event reported to David who has the murderers executed (2 Samuel 4:5-12), showing that David refuses this crime even though he benefits from his death.
H0378.portee: The character of Ish-Bosheth illustrates how God's will ultimately prevails despite human efforts to thwart it. Although Abner and his generals keep him on the throne of Israel for a few years by force, Ish-Bosheth represents a contested and illegitimate authority: God has chosen David, and no army can prevent this design. His example also shows that living according to the flesh — seeking to maintain power by arms — leads to humiliation and death, while obedience to God brings stability and unification.

sens: Man of the tribe of Manasseh during the divided monarchy
H0379.detail: Ischhod is a man from the tribe of Manasseh, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:18. He is presented as one of the sons of Hammoleketh, alongside his brothers Abiezer and Machlah. Manasseh was one of the two tribes descended from Joseph established east of the Jordan, and Ischhod is a genealogical member, although we know nothing of his deeds or particular role in the history of Israel.
H0379.origine: The name Ischhod literally means "man of majesty" or "man of splendor" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: ish ("man") and hod ("majesty, glory"). This name reflects a type of theophoric or ideal name that parents wished to bestow upon their son.
H0379.emploi: Ischhod is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:18, in a genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh. He appears in a list of descendants establishing the tribal lineages of Israel, particularly those of the transjordanian tribes. This genealogical mention is the only biblical testimony of his existence.

sens: the black and central part of the eye, through which one sees
what one protects jealously, like one's most precious possession
the deepest moment of the night, total darkness
H0380.detail:
1. The pupil is the small dark opening at the center of the eye that lets light in. It is what allows us to see. The Bible uses this concrete word to refer to this fragile and vital part of our body.

2. Because the pupil is so precious and sensitive that it is instinctively protected, the Bible uses it figuratively to denote what one cherishes above all. God says to Israel: "He kept him as the apple of his eye" (Deuteronomy 32:10), showing his jealous and watchful love. A wise man advises: "Keep my teachings as the apple of your eye" (Proverbs 7:2), inviting us to cherish wisdom as our most treasured possession.

3. Figuratively, the pupil also denotes the heart of the night, its darkest moment. When the text says "in the middle of the night and darkness" (Proverbs 7:9), it evokes the hour when the densest darkness reigns, as if the night had its own pupil from which all darkness emerges.
H0380.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "man" or "little man." Indeed, the ancients noticed that in the pupil is reflected a small image of the one who looks — like a tiny portrait. This reflected image resembles a little man, hence the name. The Hebrew word thus carries the poetic and sensitive observation of our ancestors who contemplated the mystery of sight.
H0380.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always with a strong emotional charge. Three uses describe the pupil as a symbol of jealous love and protection: God keeps Israel as the apple of his eye (Deuteronomy 32:10), the psalmist asks God to keep him likewise (Psalms 17:8), and the wise man exhorts to cherish teaching similarly (Proverbs 7:2). Two uses depict the dark depth of the night: the moment when the seducer waits for his prey "in the middle of the night and darkness" (Proverbs 7:9), and the instant when the cursed will see "his lamp go out in the midst of darkness" (Proverbs 20:20). In all cases, the word carries intensity: jealous tenderness or threatening darkness.
H0380.portee: Understanding this word helps the Christian grasp God's love as a vigilant and personal protection: God keeps us as something fragile and precious that He would never allow to be harmed. It is also a call to cherish the Word of God with the same jealous vigilance with which one protects one's sight. Finally, the image of the pupil of the night reminds us that spiritual darkness exists and is real; that is why Light must be our guard.

sens: existence or presence of something
possibility or ability
presence within a group
H0383.detail:
1. The most common meaning: to express that something exists or is present. It is a simple affirmation: "it exists," "it is there." Ezra 5:17 uses it when the king asks if there has been an order from Cyrus: "to see if there has been an order from King Cyrus."

2. The ability or possibility to do something. The word is used to say that one possesses the means or skill. Daniel 2:26 illustrates this: the king asks Daniel: "Are you able to make known to me the dream?" — literally "Is there in you [the ability] to make it known to me?"

3. To mark the presence of a reality among others, or of a person among a group. Daniel 2:11 states that no one exists among men capable of revealing the dream — "there is no one among men."

4. The existence of something divine or superior. Daniel 2:28 affirms: "there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets" — the word posits the real existence of a heavenly power in contrast to human nothingness.
H0383.origine: This Hebrew word expresses existence or presence. It comes from the verb "to be" in the sense of "to exist" or "to be found." In Hebrew and Aramaic (notably in the Aramaic passages of Daniel), it is a very ancient particle that simply states the fact: something is, exists, is found somewhere. It appears in other forms of the verb "to be" in Hebrew and takes on a particular form of biblical Aramaic here.
H0383.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of Ezra and Daniel, particularly in the Aramaic passages of Daniel. It expresses simple existence and presence. In Ezra 5:17, it seeks a historical fact: does an edict exist? In Daniel 2:10-30, it regularly returns to express human impossibility in the face of divine mystery: "there is no one" among the wise who can reveal the king's dream, "there is only God" who can do it. The word emphasizes the contrast between total human powerlessness and the presence of God. It can also mark personal ability (Daniel 2:26: "are you able?").
H0383.portee: This simple word teaches us something fundamental: faith rests on the fact that God exists and acts. When Daniel asserts "there is a God in heaven," he opposes the reality of God to the impotence of the wise of the world. For the reader, it is a reminder that God is not absent or indifferent to us — He exists, He reveals, He knows what no man can know. It is also an invitation to recognize our human limits and turn to the only one who is truly capable.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin at the time of the return from exile
H0384G.detail: Ithiel is a Benjamite who lived at the time of the restoration of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He appears in the genealogy of the inhabitants of Jerusalem who resettled there (Nehemiah 11:7), where he is presented as the son of Isaiah and the father of Maaseiah.
H0384G.origine: The name Ithiel means "God is with me" in Hebrew: it is a miniature confession of faith, expressing the trust that God accompanies the one who bears it. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common in Israel.
H0384G.emploi: Ithiel appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:7, during the enumeration of the descendants of Benjamin who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. It is simply a genealogical mention to situate his place in the restored community.

sens: disciple or interlocutor of Agur to whom the proverbs of chapter 30 are addressed
H0384H.detail: 1. Ithiel is a man to whom the wise Agur addresses his words and sayings (Proverbs 30:1). The text clearly names him for the first time: he is the person for whom Agur pronounces his proverbs, like a master speaking to a disciple or to one who comes to consult him. His name means "God is with me," which evokes a trust placed in God — an appropriate posture for one who receives and meditates on the proverbs of wisdom.
H0384H.origine: The name Ithiel contains two Hebrew elements: "with me" (iti) and "God" (el). It expresses a statement of faith: "God is with me." This type of theophoric name, which places the divine name at the heart of personal identity, is common in Israel and often indicates a pious man or someone for whom the divine presence is central.
H0384H.emploi: Ithiel appears only once in the Old Testament, in Proverbs 30:1, where Agur addresses him as the recipient of his sayings and reflections on God, creation, and wisdom. The fact that he is named at the beginning of the passage suggests that he has a certain status or a special relationship with Agur, perhaps as a disciple or a young man in search of wisdom. Beyond this mention, we know nothing of him; he does not reappear in the other books of Scripture.
H0384H.portee: The presence of Ithiel, a simple receiver of Agur's words, reminds us that biblical wisdom is always addressed to specific men and women, not just to an abstract crowd. Receiving the teaching of one who walks with God invites everyone to identify with Ithiel and to welcome the wisdom of the Lord into their own lives, trusting in the divine presence.

sens: Fourth son of the high priest Aaron
Levite in charge of priestly functions
Ancestor of a lineage of priests
H0385.detail: Ithamar is the youngest of the four sons of Aaron and Elisheba (Exodus 6:23). After the death of his two older brothers Nadab and Abihu, who offered unauthorized fire before the Lord (Leviticus 10:1-2), Ithamar becomes one of the two main leaders of worship alongside his brother Eleazar. He supervises the families of the Levites responsible for transporting and maintaining the tabernacle, notably the sons of Merari (Numbers 4:33). His descendants form an important branch of the priesthood, rivaling that of Eleazar, until the time of King David, who organizes the service of the priests according to these two lineages (1 Chronicles 24:3-6).
H0385.origine: The name Ithamar means "palm coast" or "island of palms," an image perhaps evoking a refuge or a fertile area. His father Aaron, as the founding priest of the priestly order, and his position as the fourth son, make him a man of secondary but lasting importance in the history of Israel.
H0385.emploi: Ithamar is mentioned about 21 times in the Bible, primarily in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Chronicles. He first appears in the genealogy of the sons of Aaron (Exodus 6:23; Numbers 3:2), then in the laws of worship where Moses charges him with his brother Eleazar with priestly responsibilities (Leviticus 10:6-12). In Numbers, he becomes the supervisor of the families of Merari in the service of the tabernacle (Numbers 4:28, 33). In the time of King David, his descendants form one of the two major branches of the priesthood, with eight divisions of priests (1 Chronicles 24:3-6). One of his descendants, Ezra, will become a major figure in the return from exile (Ezra 8:2).
H0385.portee: Ithamar reminds us that in God's plan, priestly responsibilities and the service of worship do not depend solely on the elders, but also on those who, like the younger sons, receive their share of the spiritual inheritance. His lineage, which has survived and thrived despite the shadow of Eleazar, shows God's faithfulness to all who serve Him humbly.

sens: That flows continuously (for a watercourse)
That subsists, endures, does not disappear
That is strong, powerful, unshakeable
That is established solidly, stable
H0386.detail:
1. A "firm" river or stream is one that flows continuously, never running dry: the psalmist speaks of "rivers that do not dry up" (Psalms 74:15), meaning watercourses that are always supplied, never dry.
2. Figuratively, firmness evokes what persists, what remains constant: when the Lord strengthens "the hands" of Joseph (Genesis 49:24), He makes them stable and enduring, capable of holding firm.
3. Applied to a person or a fortress, "firm" means strong and powerful: Jeremiah describes a "strong" nation coming from afar to conquer (Jeremiah 5:15), emphasizing its ability to resist and dominate.
4. A dwelling or a nest that is "firm" is founded solidly, established on rock so that it cannot collapse: the Kenites have a "solid dwelling" built on rock (Numbers 24:21).
H0386.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of continuity and solidity. The basic image is that of a river flowing endlessly, which explains why this term is first used to describe eternal watercourses, then extends figuratively to anything that is permanent, durable, stable, or strong. The word evokes robustness and unshakeability.
H0386.emploi: This word appears thirteen times in the poetic and prophetic books of the Bible. It is first used literally for rivers and streams that never run dry (Psalms 74:15; Amos 5:24); then it shifts to figuratively describe the solidity of a structure or the strength of a position (Numbers 24:21; Jeremiah 50:44). The context shows that "firm" expresses either reassuring permanence (the stability of the divine flow) or formidable power (the strength of a nation or an adversary). In Genesis 49:24, it characterizes the warrior's bow that remains "firm," meaning capable of holding firm under tension.
H0386.portee: Meditating on this firmness helps the believer understand that God is constant and reliable, like a river that never runs dry. It also reminds us that true strength is not that of man, but that which God grants to those who rely on Him, like Joseph whose arms are strengthened by the Mighty One of Jacob.

sens: Wise man of the time of the united monarchy, brother of Heman, Calcol, and Darda
Author of a psalm of wisdom and prayer
H0387G.detail:
1. Ethan the Ezrahite is mentioned for the first time in 1 Kings 4:31 as a man renowned for his great wisdom, compared to Solomon: he is cited alongside Heman, Calcol, and Darda, all sons of Mahol, forming a group of sages from the time of the united monarchy in Israel. The text emphasizes that Solomon was superior to him in wisdom, highlighting the extraordinary excellence of David's son.
2. Ethan is also the author of a psalm (Psalm 89), titled "A Song of Ethan the Ezrahite," where he expresses his trust in God and recalls the divine promises made to the house of David despite present trials.
H0387G.origine: The name Ethan means "firm," "durable," or "enduring" in Hebrew. It designates a man living in the time of the united monarchy, son of Mahol according to 1 Kings 4:31. The Bible mentions several men bearing this name — a wise Ezrahite, a grandson of Judah father of Azariah, a Kohathite, and a Merarite son of Kushiah — but the references in the Segond 1910 relate to the sage of Solomon's time.
H0387G.emploi: Ethan appears twice in the provided references. In 1 Kings 4:31, he represents a member of the group of great sages of Israel during Solomon's time, known for his intellectual excellence and renown that extended to neighboring nations. In Psalm 89, he is presented as the author or composer of a song, confirming his status as a wise man and servant of God capable of meditating on divine promises and expressing Israel's faith.
H0387G.portee: Ethan embodies human wisdom in Israel and reminds us that God values intelligence and deep reflection: the psalm he composed invites the reader to meditate on God's faithfulness despite adverse appearances. His example also shows that Solomon, to whom he is compared, receives incomparable wisdom — a divine gift that places him beyond the greatest sages of his time.

sens: son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah
father of Azaria
H0387H.detail:
1. Ethan is a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the five sons of Zerah mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2:6. He is part of the genealogical lineage of Judah and is among the ancestors of the Israelite people long before the establishment of the monarchy.
2. He is the father of Azaria, as indicated in 1 Chronicles 2:8, which lists his direct descendants in the genealogy of Judah.
H0387H.origine: The name Ethan means "enduring" or "persevering" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of solidity and permanence. This character belongs to the genealogy of Judah and is part of the transmission of the Israelite lineage through generations.
H0387H.emploi: Ethan appears twice in the Bible, exclusively in the first book of Chronicles in chapters 2:6 and 2:8. These two mentions are part of the genealogies of the tribe of Judah listed at the beginning of the book, establishing the links of filiation between generations. He is presented as the son of Zerah and the father of Azaria, two strategic positions in the genealogical tree of Judah.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi during the divided monarchy
H0387I.detail: Ethan is a Levite mentioned in the genealogies from the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between north and south. He appears in 1 Chronicles 6:42 as the son of Zimma and the father of Iddo, listed in the lineage of the descendants of Levi responsible for temple service. The name may refer to several characters among God's people, but this one is clearly identified by his genealogy in the priestly tribe of Levi.
H0387I.origine: The name Ethan comes from a Hebrew root meaning "durable" or "constant," evoking solidity and permanence. It is a theophoric name reflecting faith in God's stability. Several men bore this name in Israel's history, including a sage renowned for his wisdom and other Levites involved in temple worship.
H0387I.emploi: Ethan primarily appears in the genealogical lists of Chronicles, which trace the official history of Israel after the exile. In 1 Chronicles 6:42, he is situated in the genealogy of the Kohathite or Merarite Levites, descendants of those who served in the tabernacle and then the temple. These enumerations show the importance that the authors of Chronicles placed on the continuity of the priestly lineage and the role of the Levites in Israel's worship life. The character himself is not described in action but simply presented as a link in the genealogical chain.

sens: A chief Levite musician during the united monarchy
Son of Kushaiah, of the tribe of Merari
H0387J.detail:
1. Ethan is a high-ranking Levite during the reign of King David, responsible for the music of the Temple. He is mentioned alongside Heman and Asaph, the other two great musicians of Israel: all three play the bronze cymbals during major celebrations, particularly when the Ark of the Covenant is transported to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:19). He is a man of prestige, whose name appears several times in the genealogical lists of the Levites.
2. Ethan belongs to the lineage of Merari, one of the three major families of Levites. He is the son of Kushaiah (also called Kishi) and the father of several sons who will also play a role in the Temple worship (1 Chronicles 6:44). His descendants are thus integrated into the structure of divine service.
H0387J.origine: The name Ethan means "enduring" in Hebrew, that is, "one who remains" or "who perseveres" — the idea of lasting solidity and firmness. It is a name well-suited for a man established in a position of responsibility. Ethan is also known by the name Jeduthun, another title recognized in the Old Testament for this same Levite musician.
H0387J.emploi: Ethan is mentioned three times in the biblical text, all occurrences appearing in the first book of Chronicles. First in the genealogy of the Merarite Levites (1 Chronicles 6:44), where he is precisely identified by his family line. Then, during the solemn installation of the Ark of the Covenant under David, he is named among the three masters of music chosen to lead the liturgy (1 Chronicles 15:17). Finally, he is recalled as one of the three musicians playing the cymbals during this same ceremony (1 Chronicles 15:19). His mentions reflect a dual role: he is both a genealogist and a prominent liturgical musician.
H0387J.portee: Ethan embodies the role of musicians and singers in Israel's worship. His importance underscores that praise and music are not secondary additions to prayer but a central part of Temple service — a truth confirmed by the Christian Church, for whom singing and music remain essential to worship. The fact that his names and genealogy are carefully preserved also shows that every function in God's service has its own dignity.

sens: seventh month of the ancient Hebrew calendar
month corresponding to October-November
month during which the permanent springs still flowed
H0388.detail: Ethanim is the name of the seventh month of the Jewish religious year. This name means "the enduring ones" or "the permanent ones," as it is during this month that the springs and streams continued to flow in the land of Israel, unlike the summer months when drought was more intense. It was during this month that King Solomon inaugurated the Temple built in Jerusalem: "All the men of Israel assembled before King Solomon in the month of Ethanim, which is the seventh month, during the feast" (1 Kings 8:2). This month approximately corresponds to our months of October and November.
H0388.origine: The name Ethanim comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to endure" or "to be durable." This name reflects the climatic observation of the ancient Israelites: it is the time of year when the waterways remained active, unlike the summer drought. The ancient Hebrew calendar bore the names of the months based on natural or religious phenomena; Ethanim is a characteristic example of this.
H0388.emploi: Ethanim appears only once in the Bible in 1 Kings 8:2, during the description of the dedication of the Temple by Solomon. This passage indicates that it was in this seventh month that the king summoned all the elders of Israel and all the leaders of the tribes to inaugurate the newly constructed sanctuary. It is a key moment in the religious history of Israel.

sens: Expresses a strong affirmation, a certainty
Introduces a restriction or an exception
Marks a reservation, a correction, a contrast
Introduces a conditional clause or a reservation
H0389.detail:
1. This is a word that reinforces what is being affirmed, as if to say "it is really true." In Genesis 9:4, God says to Noah: "Only, you shall not eat flesh with its soul, with its blood" — the word emphasizes the absolute importance of this prohibition.

2. It marks a limit or an exclusion: this is it and nothing else, everything else is excluded. In 1 Samuel 20:39, "David alone understood the matter" means that only David and Jonathan understood, and no one else. In Numbers 18:15, "Only you shall redeem the firstborn of man" means: it is only for humans that redemption must be made.

3. It expresses a nuance, a gentle objection, or an unexpected turn. In 2 Chronicles 30:11, "Nevertheless, some men humbled themselves" — the word suggests: "despite the difficulties, still."
H0389.origine: This word comes from a root that likely means "limitation" or "solitude." It is mainly used to restrict or reinforce a statement. In Hebrew, it is a very flexible adverb: depending on the context, it can insist ("really") or reserve ("only"). It is very frequent throughout the entire Bible, especially for the laws of the Pentateuch.
H0389.emploi: This word appears 157 times in the Hebrew Bible, very often in the laws of the Pentateuch (Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy). Its uses vary: to reinforce a prescription (Exodus 12:15: "Only, on the first day you shall remove the leaven"), to exclude (Numbers 1:49: "Only, you shall not number the tribe of Levi"), to correct a previous statement (1 Kings 11:39: "Nevertheless, I will afflict the descendants of David"). It is also found in the Psalms and wisdom literature to express a strong conviction (Psalms 62:6: "Yes, my soul, trust in God"). Each meaning, restrictive or affirmative, is read in its immediate context.
H0389.portee: This word reminds us that the word of God sets clear limits and conditions. It invites the reader to listen not only to what is commanded but also to what is reserved, excluded, or to come. It is a word of sobriety and subtlety: it says that God does not give everything at once, and that there are boundaries to respect.

sens: City in northern Babylonia, ancient center of power
H0390.detail: Accad is an ancient city in northern Babylonia (Middle Eastern region). It appears in Genesis 10:10 as one of the first cities of Nimrod's kingdom, alongside Babel, Erech, and Calneh. It is an important political center in ancient history.
H0390.origine: The name Accad refers to a real historical site in ancient Mesopotamia, also known as Akkad. It recalls the Akkadian Empire that dominated the region in the third millennium BC. The Hebrew word אַכַּד reflects this famous city and the civilization that developed there.
H0390.emploi: Accad appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 10:10. This verse mentions it as one of the four great cities founded by Nimrod in the land of Shinar (Babylonia). The Bible presents it as a seat of ancient power and an important element in the early history of humanity after the Flood.

sens: Water source that dries up or cannot be relied upon
That which disappoints and leaves one without help when needed
Deceptive or treacherous thing
H0391.detail:
1. A deceptive spring is a water source that disappears or dries up when one is counting on it for drinking: it seems to promise water, but it does not provide it. Jeremiah complains to God that He is like a deceptive spring to him, a water that is uncertain (Jeremiah 15:18).
2. By extension, the word designates anything that deceives expectation and leaves someone without help or support at a critical moment. The houses of Aczib are called a deceptive spring for the kings of Israel: the promised city provides support and refuge, but it does not hold them (Micah 1:14).
3. The image is enriched with moral meaning: it is a deceptive, lying, treacherous thing, upon which one cannot rely. It evokes deception and disappointment, not only the absence of help but the deliberate or apparent failure of one who promises aid.
H0391.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to deceive" or "to disappoint." The central image is that of a spring that does not flow when one needs it — it is a vivid metaphor to express deception and unfaithfulness. The root first evokes dryness and absence, then takes on a moral meaning: that which disappoints expectation, that which does not keep its promise.
H0391.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in contexts of complaint or threat. Jeremiah accuses God of being like a deceptive spring in the midst of his suffering: it is an accusatory question, where the prophet asks why God does not comfort him. In Micah, the same image applies to the city of Aczib, which was supposed to be a refuge but is not for the kings. Both uses revolve around disappointment and failure: something or someone expected to be faithful turns out to be deceptive.
H0391.portee: This word helps the reader to name the spiritual experience of disappointment and doubt. Jeremiah does not hesitate to tell God that he feels betrayed; this word legitimizes the cry of the heart in the face of God's apparent absence. It teaches us that we can express our frustration, our feeling of being left without help, before God. It is also a warning: do not rely on human promises or worldly securities that may disappoint us like a spring that dries up.

sens: City in the mountainous region of western Judah
H0392G.detail: Aczib is a locality in the territory of Judah, listed among the cities of the Shephelah (the lowland and hilly coastal area) in Joshua 15:44. The prophet Micah mentions it as an example of the divine punishments suffered by the cities of Israel, playing on its Hebrew name: its houses would become a source of deception or disappointment for the kings, which recalls the meaning of the name Aczib, "deception."
H0392G.origine: The Hebrew name אַכְזִיב (akhziv) literally means "deception" or "disappointment." This city of Judah bears a name that evokes the idea of lying or falsehood. The prophet Micah precisely exploits this play on words when he prophesies against the city.
H0392G.emploi: Aczib appears twice in the Bible. First in Joshua 15:44, it is listed among the cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the promised land. Then, the prophet Micah, around the 8th century BC, uses it as an example in his oracle of doom against the cities of Israel: in Micah 1:14, he plays on the name of Aczib to announce that this city will be nothing but a source of deception or disappointment for the kings who place their hopes there.
H0392G.portee: Micah's play on the name of Aczib reminds us that human securities and political alliances that do not rely on God are deceptive. The prophet invites us to place our trust in God rather than in fortified cities or earthly kings.

sens: coastal city in the territory of Asher in the Promised Land
H0392H.detail: 1. Aczib is a small coastal city located in the territory assigned to the tribe of Asher in the Promised Land (Joshua 19:29). It is mentioned during the delineation of Asher's borders, situated between Ramah and Hosa, near Tyre and the Mediterranean Sea. At the time of conquest, the tribe of Asher failed to drive out the inhabitants of Aczib (Judges 1:31), which shows that, like several other cities, it was not completely subdued despite its allocation to the Israelites.
H0392H.origine: The name Aczib means "deception" or "lie" in Hebrew, deriving from a root expressing the idea of deceit or falsehood. This name may be ironic or reflect a characteristic of the city, but it remains geographically a small coastal locality in northern Israel, in the Phoenician region.
H0392H.emploi: Aczib appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. It is mentioned in Joshua 19:29 during the description of the borders of the territory of Asher after the conquest of Canaan. It then appears in Judges 1:31, where it is noted that Asher could not drive out the indigenous inhabitants, contrary to the promise of complete conquest. Aczib thus represents one of the cities that the Israelites did not fully conquer.
H0392H.portee: Aczib illustrates a reality of God's people after entering the Promised Land: although lands were assigned to them, the conquest was not total. This reminds us that obedience to God requires initiative and perseverance, and that spiritual half-measures leave obstacles in our walk of faith.

sens: Showing brutality and violence without mercy
Acting with relentless harshness
Possessing a fierce and wild nature
Lacking compassion in actions or words
H0393.detail:
1. The word primarily describes physical brutality and merciless violence: it is the action of deliberately causing harm without restraint. When Job says that God has become "cruel" against him, he evokes this brutal force that strikes him "with the strength of your hand" (Job 30:21), a violence that does not shy away from anything.

2. It also refers to the ferocity of a wild and merciless nature: the venom of the serpent is "cruel" (Deuteronomy 32:33) because it kills without compassion, and even the "cruel" ostriches of the desert (Lamentations 4:3) abandon their young, unlike other animals. It is a harshness that opposes all tenderness.

3. Finally, the word can evoke a kind of boldness or recklessness in the face of danger: no one is "bold enough" to provoke Leviathan (Job 41:1), this fearsome monster that cannot be confronted. Here, "cruel" borders on the meaning of "fierce" or "formidable."
H0393.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that suggests brutality and lack of pity. It is a term of brute force opposed to compassion. It belongs to the semantic field of animal ferocity and unrestrained violence, from wild beasts to the hardness of the human heart.
H0393.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe extreme harshness. In Deuteronomy and Job, it applies to the violence of God or that of nature (the venom, wild animals). In Lamentations, it characterizes the people of Israel who have become hard and unfeeling due to famine and siege. The context is invariably one of suffering, loss of natural tenderness, or destructive force against which one is defenseless.
H0393.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize the reality of evil and suffering: God Himself may seem cruel to those who suffer, and the human heart can become as hard as that of fierce beasts. It is a call to examine our own hearts and to guard against this hardness that ignores compassion. Understanding cruelty as the Bible evokes it is also to grasp how much divine grace and mercy are necessary for us.

sens: Without pity or mercy towards those who suffer
Acting with harshness and wickedness
Violent, merciless in action
Ignoring compassion
H0394.detail: 1. The word describes one who is devoid of pity: they do not seek to spare suffering, but rather to prolong or intensify it. In Proverbs 5:9, the cruel man robs the vigor and years of his victim, showing a hardness of heart that destroys. 2. It is a disposition of the heart manifested by wicked and merciless acts. Proverbs 11:17 contrasts the good man, who benefits himself, with the cruel man who "troubles his own flesh" — that is, who sinks into misery through his own hardness. 3. It is also seen in those who commit violence: Jeremiah 6:23 describes cruel soldiers "without mercy," like a roaring sea, ready to devastate. 4. It is a trait of the heart that ignores compassion towards the weak: Proverbs 12:10 contrasts the righteous who cares for his livestock with the wicked whose "insides are cruel," meaning devoid of pity even for animals.
H0394.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of brute force devoid of feeling. It is akin to the image of ferocity or bestiality: the one who is cruel is as if deprived of human heart, reduced to pure violence. The biblical context often places it in parallel with the absence of mercy and compassion, vices opposed to the very nature of God.
H0394.emploi: The word appears about eight times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in Proverbs and the prophets. In Proverbs, it describes dispositions of the human heart — that of the libertine (5:9), the wicked (11:17, 12:10), the rebellious (17:11) — and shows how cruelty first destroys the one who practices it. In the prophets (Isaiah 13:9, Jeremiah 6:23, 30:14, 50:42), it qualifies enemies of God or divine punishments: cruelty becomes the instrument of the Lord's anger against sin. The context varies between the moral portrait of the wicked and the description of divine judgment.
H0394.portee: This word invites the believer to examine their own heart: am I cruel towards those I could abuse — the weak, the dependent, animals? Proverbs shows that cruelty first destroys ourselves before it destroys others. It also reminds us that God Himself, far from being indifferent to evil, exercises judgment without pity against sin: it is a warning to repentance.

sens: Hardness of heart, absence of pity
Ferocity, merciless violence
Jealousy that consumes and destroys
H0395.detail: 1. Cruelty is the total absence of compassion, a heart closed to the suffering of others. It is a hardness that drives the one afflicted to do harm without remorse. In Proverbs 27:4, jealousy is presented as more cruel than fury or anger: it gnaws at the one who experiences it and drives them to destructive acts. 2. The word also evokes the ferocity of a wild beast, a violence without restraint or limit. Cruelty ignores all restraint, all human feeling. 3. In this biblical passage, the cruelty of jealousy surpasses that of all other violent feelings: it is untamable and devours everything in its path.
H0395.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses bitterness and hardness. It is formed with a suffix that makes it an abstract noun, designating the quality of one who is cruel. Cruelty is presented in the Bible as an absence of the fear of God and respect for His creation.
H0395.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 27:4. It describes jealousy as the most cruel of passions: more destructive than fury, more relentless than impassioned anger. The context shows that cruelty is not merely an action, but a state of the heart that consumes the one who bears it and threatens those around them.
H0395.portee: Cruelty reveals a heart distant from God. By reading that jealousy is cruel, the believer is called to examine their own heart and to reject any destructive feeling. The Bible constantly opposes this hardness to the mercy and compassion that God demands from His people.

sens: that which is eaten, that which nourishes the body
a meal, the act of eating together
the strength or energy provided by food
H0396.detail:
1. Food is what one eats to live and sustain oneself. In the account of Elijah, the prophet receives miraculous food — bread and water — that allows him to walk for forty days without any other provisions, as recounted in 1 Kings 19:8.
2. The word can also refer to a meal, a moment when people eat together. It is the very act of eating and sharing a table.
3. Food also symbolizes the vital force it provides: it is not just sustenance, but the physical power it gives to act and survive.
H0396.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root אכל (akhal), which means "to eat." Akḥilah is the noun derived from this root: it is the food itself, or the act of eating transformed into a thing. This same root is found in verbs and other nouns related to the table in biblical Hebrew.
H0396.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 19:8. It describes the supernatural food that the angel gives to Elijah on Mount Horeb: bread and a jar of water. This food is not ordinary, as it sustains the prophet for forty days and forty nights of walking — a reminder of Moses' journey to Sinai and a manifestation of God's power to nourish His servant.
H0396.portee: This passage shows that God provides for our most basic needs and gives us the strength to continue His mission, even beyond what nature allows. Elijah's supernatural food invites the believer to trust God for daily resources and for the spiritual vigor of their faith journey.

sens: Philistine king of the city of Gath
Protector of David in flight
H0397.detail: Achish is a Philistine king who reigns over Gath, one of the main cities of Philistia. He appears in the story of David fleeing from King Saul. Achish welcomes David to his court and trusts him, to the point of making him responsible for his personal security (1 Samuel 28:2). David feigns madness before Achish to escape his suspicions (1 Samuel 21:14), which leads the king to drive him away, then to take him back into favor. Later, David settles in Ziklag, a city that Achish entrusts to him, and lives there for several years as a vassal of the Philistine king (1 Samuel 27:5-6). Their relationship remains complex: Achish respects David and protects him, but the other Philistine princes suspect him of disloyalty. At the end of Saul's reign, Achish wants David to fight alongside the Philistines against Israel, but the military leaders oppose this (1 Samuel 29:6).
H0397.origine: The name Achish literally means "I will darken" or "I will terrify," or possibly "just a man." He is also called Abimelech ("my father is king"), which may indicate a royal title or nickname. The name suggests either an image of terror and power or an ironic humility before the gods.
H0397.emploi: Achish appears in about 20 passages in 1 Samuel and 1 Kings, almost exclusively in the account of David's flight (chapters 21, 27-29). He is the only Philistine king named individually in the Hebrew Bible. In chapter 21, David seeks refuge with him to escape Saul, feigns madness, and is sent away. In chapter 27, David voluntarily returns, places himself under his protection, and receives Ziklag. In chapter 29, on the eve of the battle of Gilboa, Achish asks David to fight with him against Israel, but the other Philistine generals refuse. These passages show how an enemy of Israel can be just and favorable to David, and how David navigates between two worlds.
H0397.portee: The story of Achish illustrates that God can protect His people through unexpected means, including the kindness of an enemy. It also shows the careful faithfulness: David must remain loyal to God while living under the tutelage of a Philistine king, an uncomfortable but necessary situation. For the Christian reader, it reminds us that God governs all things and can provide help from surprising sources.

sens: to absorb food through the mouth
H0398.detail:
1. To eat: this is the primary and most common meaning of the verb. It is found as early as the first chapters of Genesis, where God commands man to eat from the fruit of the trees in the garden (Genesis 2:16) and where Adam and Eve are tempted to eat the forbidden fruit (Genesis 3:6). One eats bread, meat, fruits — it is the basic act of nourishment. Aaron and his sons eat the flesh of the sacrifice at the entrance of the tent (Leviticus 8:31). Jehoiachin eats at the king's table for the rest of his life (Jeremiah 52:33).

2. To devour: the verb is used for a violent and destructive act, especially when animals eat, or when fire consumes something. Fire devours the land (Exodus 3:2), locusts devour the harvest (Exodus 10:5). Figuratively, the sword devours, violence and oppression devour — the image is one of a power that destroys and annihilates, absorbing everything in its path.

3. To consume: destruction through progressive consumption. Oppression and misery "eat" a person, meaning they wear them down, exhaust them, gnaw at them from within. This evokes the idea of a force that gradually reduces what it reaches, like fire consuming wood.

4. To nourish: the verb takes on this active meaning when one makes someone else eat, when one sustains them. Pharaoh nourishes Joseph and his family during the famine (Genesis 45:18). It is the act of providing for someone else's sustenance, keeping them alive through food.
H0398.origine: The verb אָכַל (akhal) is a very ancient and common Semitic root. Its basic image is that of the mouth absorbing food. The word is related to Aramaic forms and other Semitic languages. In Aramaic, we find אֲכַל (akhal) with the same meaning. The root has no known deeper etymology: it is a primitive word from the vocabulary of daily life, likely imitated from the gesture or sound of eating.
H0398.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, used over 700 times. It appears in all historical, poetic, and prophetic books. The basic meaning — to eat food — overwhelmingly dominates (Genesis 2:16, Leviticus 8:31, Jeremiah 52:33). But from the Genesis account, the verb enriches: eating the forbidden fruit becomes an act of transgression laden with consequences (Genesis 3). The verb also applies to animals that eat, insects, and fire that devours (Exodus 10:5, Exodus 3:2). Figuratively, it expresses destruction, exhaustion, oppression. The variety of Hebrew forms (Qal, Niphal, Piel, Hiphil) allows for differentiation between eating oneself, being eaten, and making someone else eat — all essential nuances for understanding the action.
H0398.portee: This verb reminds us that food is a gift from God — it is by His permission that we eat (Genesis 2:16). The contrast between eating what is permitted and eating what is forbidden shows that the act of eating is never purely physical: it involves obedience or disobedience. The figurative sense of the verb — to devour, consume, destroy — warns us that certain powers gnaw at and exhaust humanity: oppression, injustice, sin. Understanding these nuances helps grasp how the Bible speaks of sin, grace, and our dependence on God.

sens: To consume food
To devour, to consume eagerly
To accuse, to slander someone
H0399.detail:
1. The primary and most common meaning is simply "to eat": to absorb food. It is the basic act of nourishment, practiced by both humans and animals. Nebuchadnezzar, reduced to an animal state, "ate grass like the oxen" (Daniel 4:33).
2. "To devour" pushes the image further: to eat voraciously, eagerly, often to destroy or completely consume. The beasts in the vision devoured what remained under their feet (Daniel 7:7): they did not just eat; they ravaged.
3. In a figurative sense, "to accuse" or "to slander" comes from the image of devouring with words: to eat someone is to criticize them fiercely, to destroy them through slander. The Chaldeans who "accused" the Jews (Daniel 3:8) were "eating" them verbally by maliciously denouncing them.
H0399.origine: This verb belongs to the ancient Semitic family for "to eat." Its basic image is very concrete: the absorption of food. When it extends to the figurative sense of "to slander" or "to accuse," it is through a common metaphor in many languages: to devour someone with words is to criticize them with an aggressiveness that "consumes" them. In Aramaic, as in Hebrew and other Semitic languages, this verb is one of the oldest and most fundamental in the vocabulary.
H0399.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the book of Daniel (3:8, 4:33, 6:24, 7:5, 7:7, 7:19, 7:23). It is used first in the literal sense: Nebuchadnezzar "eats" grass (4:33), the animals in the vision "eat" and "devour" (7:5, 7:7, 7:19). But Daniel also uses the verb in the figurative sense for accusation: the Chaldeans "accuse" (or literally "eat") the Jews and Daniel (3:8, 6:24). This extension of meaning, from the concrete to the figurative, shows how a violent physical action can express verbal aggression.
H0399.portee: This word reminds us of the destructive power of words: "to eat" someone by accusing them is a form of real violence, as serious as physical devastation. It also invites us to recognize that our criticisms, our slanders, our accusations gnaw and destroy like a fire. Conversely, it urges us to be vigilant: not to let ourselves be "devoured" by gossipers, but also not to "eat" our brothers with our malicious words.

sens: Maritime port on the Red Sea
Strategic city at the southeastern tip of Israel
Power struggle between Judah and its neighbors
H0359A.detail:
1. Elath is a port located on the northeastern arm of the Red Sea, an important coastal city for maritime trade. It was here that Solomon built ships and from where his trading expeditions set out (1 Kings 9:26).
2. The city was located at the southeastern tip of the territory of Israel, near Ezion-geber. It marked the boundary of the country toward the desert and the southeastern regions (Deuteronomy 2:8).
3. Elath was a power struggle: King Azaria rebuilt it and reclaimed it for Judah (2 Kings 14:22), but King Rezin of Syria later conquered it and expelled the Jews (2 Kings 16:6), showing how this prosperous city was coveted by neighboring powers.
H0359A.origine: The name literally means "grove of majestic trees" or "grove of lofty trees" according to ancient etymology. It is a place name that likely describes the characteristic landscape of this coastal region.
H0359A.emploi: Elath appears three times in the Old Testament, always in historical passages. In Deuteronomy 2:8, Moses mentions Elath during the crossing of the desert, simply as a geographical landmark. In 2 Kings 14:22 and 16:6, the city becomes a political issue: King Azaria reannexes it to Judah, but the Syrian king Rezin soon tears it away, illustrating the constant conflicts of the ancient Near East for control of maritime trade routes.
H0359A.portee: Elath reminds us that the prosperity of Israel was linked to its control of trade routes and ports. The loss of Elath symbolizes the gradual decline of the power of the kingdom of Judah in the face of its enemies, a lesson on the importance of strength and unity to preserve what God has entrusted.
